articles.title_orig: Amoris laetitia: Pastoral experiences in Asia and challenges of digital world
articles.title_zh: Amoris laetitia: Pastoral experiences in Asia and challenges of digital world
articles.content_orig:
Families today are âa challenging mosaic of diverse realities, marked by joys, hopes, struggles and wounds. The family is not only a place to which the Church brings the Gospel. It is also a place from which the Gospel comes alive â from one generation to another, from one family to another, and from families to society.â
Cardinal Filipe Neri Ferrão, Metropolitan Archbishop of Goa and Daman, opened his address with this reflection at the start of the second day of Pope Leo XIVâs meeting with the heads of the Eastern Churches and the presidents of the Bishopsâ Conferences, ten years after Amoris laetitia .
The Indian Cardinal addressed the theme âFamilies today: reality, beauty and challenges. Discerning the signs of the times through the experience of families and the Churchâs pastoral commitment today.â
He invited participants in the meeting, conducted in a synodal style, to ask themselves in their discernment: âWhat is the Holy Spirit asking the Church to change?â
This concerned ânot only in what we do for the families, but in how we understand, accompany and empower them as protagonists of the Gospel and as enduring loci of Godâs revelation.â
Drawing on his experience as a pastor in Asia, particularly in India, Cardinal Neri Ferrão acknowledged that families had changed in their identity, nature, and composition, with smaller households, new forms of cohabitation, and interreligious marriages.
Families were increasingly on the move, and many faced economic insecurity, poverty, unemployment, and uncertainty about the future.
âChristian families in many parts of India and Asia,â the Cardinal stressed, âmust also live amid growing religious polarisation and hostility, making the public expression and transmission of faith increasingly difficult.â
Yet, these families also offered the Church beauty through their care for children, the elderly, the sick, and vulnerable people. Even amid poverty and uncertainty, the Cardinal explained, âour families continue to create positive spaces for joy and hope.â
Following the publication of Amoris laetitia , he recalled, the Churches in India and across Asia âlistened first to families,â and that listening âshaped how we walk with them. We now see marriage preparation as the start of a lifelong journey, offer spiritual renewal and counselling to couples and children, and keep forming families and lay leaders over time.â
He stressed that pastoral ministry needed to move âfrom mission to families to mission among families.â Families were not simply recipients of assistance but, in his words, âthe Church's partners in mission.â
Cardinal Neri Ferrão concluded by recounting the experience of a priest who had begun family ministry in his parish not with a program, but by visiting a family experiencing underlying difficulties in communication between the parents and between them and their children. It had begun with âa conversation and a willingness to listen.â
The second speaker, Vincenzo Rosito, Professor of the History and Culture of Family Institutions at the Pontifical Lateran University and Vice Dean of the Pontifical John Paul II Theological Institute for Marriage and Family Sciences, summed up his address with questions to guide participantsâ synodal discernment.
He began with an invitation inspired by Pope Leo XIVâs reflections in the encyclical Magnifica humanitas : âLet each of us be mindful of the relationships we build within our own families and within the Church.â
Professor Rosito stressed that âfamily practices, in fact, help us to understand how churches and families learn from one another. Both the Church and the family, in fact, learn through the practices of their daily lives.â
He then offered a question for participants to consider as a father, mother, theologian, or pastor: âAm I able to recognise and share with others at least one new thing that I have learnt to do, or to do differently, in recent years of my family or pastoral life?â
Changes in family life, Prof. Rosito explained, âare not problemsâ but âhuman activities.â Recalling Amoris laetitia , he presented them as an opportunity, as concrete processes âin which individuals and families act, react, learn and develop new resources.â
âConsider, for example,â the political philosopher continued, âhow the use of new digital technologies is transforming the daily habits of families and the way children are brought up.â
The family and the Church, Prof. Rosito continued, âlearn together through change.â He drew on the Gospel image of Jesus, Joseph, and Maryâs flight into Egypt.
He noted that today, âdrawing on the experiences of refugee and migrant families, some Christian communities are re-establishing themselves as ârefuge churchesââ for those arriving in a new land or making a long journey.
He also addressed the tragedy of violence shared by many families: âThe insecurity stemming from social and political violence is a worrying reality that many Churches must deal with today, in their daily lives.â Such insecurity, he warned, could âeven devour family bonds and church relationships themselves.â
Josephâs dream was also part of the experience of this flight.
âTo dream, to imagine new forms for the Church,â Prof. Rosito concluded, âalso means renewing what we already do. To imagine the Church means being willing to learn from one another, whilst we are transformed together, as churches and as families.â
His final question for discernment was therefore: âWhat do we need, amidst the light and shadow of today, to learn and imagine new ways of being a family and new ways of being the Church?â

Amazon is launching a new lineup of tablets that bear almost no resemblance to any tablet Amazon has ever launched before. They’re not even called Fire, the name Amazon has used for its tablets for the last 15 years. They’re called Alexa Tablets, and they’re designed to do two things: bring Alexa Plus to the center of your whole computing life, and be straight-up excellent tablets.
The most important thing about these new tablets’ software? They run Android. Full, Google Play-supported, all-the-apps Android. There are plenty of preloaded Amazon apps, of course, and some built-in ways to quickly access Prime Video content or shop for basically anything anywhere at any time, but it’s finally offering a proper Android experience. Panos Panay, Amazon’s SVP in charge of all things hardware and Alexa, tells me that “Google Play was a necessity, end of story.”
But Panay picked Android as the second most important thing about the Alexa Tablet. The first, he says, is the hardware. The Alexa Tablet is two and a half years in the making, Panay says, and he directed the team to start completely fresh in their tablet design. “Start from zero, don’t use any components we’ve ever used,” he says he told them. “Just ask, what is it? What is a great piece of hardware and what is it supposed to do?”
There are three devices in the Alexa Tablet lineup, all of which go on sale October 14th. The Tablet 8 has an 8.7-inch screen, starts at $229.99 , and seems mostly designed for reading; the Tablet 11 has an 11-inch screen, starts at $329.99, and is more for watching stuff. They’re aimed squarely at the iPad Mini and base iPad, and seem nice enough. But the biggest device in the lineup, the one Panay really wants to tell me about, is the one he thinks really shows off what Amazon is doing here.
It’s called the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, and it starts at $499 . It’s 6.5mm thick and weighs 550 grams — a little thicker and a little lighter than the latest 13-inch iPad Pro — and comes with either 8 or 16 gigs of RAM and either 128 or 256 gigs of storage. It runs a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor, a chip you might have found in a high-end phone a year or so ago. All these specs are… fine. Good enough to run an Android tablet, but nothing to write home about.
The feature that really matters, Panay says, is the screen. Panay has this concept of the “one thing,” a single feature on a product that absolutely cannot be compromised on, no matter what. Make tradeoffs where you need to, he tells his team, but not on the one thing. “And the one thing on this product was, let’s go make the perfect screen.”
That screen is a 12.5-inch, 2800 x 1840 display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz and 500 nits of brightness. Its 3:2 aspect ratio, Panay says, is perfect for running two Android apps side by side. And on the most expensive, $549 model Alexa Tablet, the screen comes with what Amazon calls a Nanomatte display. The company partnered with Corning to actually etch a unique texture into the glass itself that is meant to be richer, higher contrast, and less prone to glare than a typical display. The process sounds similar to Apple’s excellent nano-texture finishes , but Amazon seems to believe its method comes with even fewer tradeoffs in contrast and sharpness. I haven’t seen the device in person yet, but The Verge ’s Terrence O’Brien has, and it sounds like it has a chance to be as good as advertised.
The screen also adapts to what you’re doing on the tablet. If you launch the Kindle app, it turns off blue lights to make the reading experience warmer and more serene; if you start reading comics, it’ll render them extra glossy. Amazon understands well that tablets are primarily consumption devices — and the company is very happy to optimize for your time in Kindle and Prime Video.
The Alexa Tablet isn’t just for watching and reading, though. Amazon also made a keyboard case and a stylus, and Panay says he hopes people will use it as a secondary or even primary computer. He also hopes you’ll use it to do Alexa things. Amazon has been working on the LLM-powered version of its assistant for the last few years, and believes Alexa Plus can be more than just a smart home assistant. (Our testing suggests… otherwise.) You’ll be able to ask Alexa about anything you see on the screen, and the chatbot will try to offer recommendations, find information, and, of course, try to sell you anything it can find on Amazon.com . On these devices, Alexa Plus appears to be nearly as pervasive as Gemini or Siri on other tablets, and that’s precisely the point.
It has always made sense for Amazon to make tablets. But for so many years, the company that has seemed to be happy to simply make everything as cheap as possible in the hopes you’ll sign up for Prime and buy some stuff in the store. Trying to actually make great tablets seems new, and frankly a little surprising. But if it got the screen right, and made the right tradeoffs elsewhere, Amazon might finally have a proper iPad competitor.

articles.title_orig: NASA photo of Mars dawn reveals cliffs in unprecedented detail
articles.title_zh: NASA photo of Mars dawn reveals cliffs in unprecedented detail
articles.content_orig:
The captivating shapes of wind-carved crags called yardangs are revealed in this zoomed-in crop of a broader panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover on Aug. 11, 2026. Scientists are eager to learn more about how the yardang layer formed.
Sunlight illuminates wind-carved cliffs in a dramatic new image.
A newly released panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity rover offers the most detailed view yet of distant, wind-carved Martian cliffs, highlighting features the mission’s scientists have long been waiting to see up close. The scene was snapped at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, showing striking blue hues in the foreground as bright morning light illuminates crags known as yardangs on the horizon.
The panorama was captured by Curiosity’s Mastcam on Aug. 11, the 4,982nd Martian day, or sol, of the mission, and comprises six individual images that were stitched together after being sent to Earth. Unlike most of Curiosity’s Mastcam images, this one was processed without white balancing, preserving the early morning appearance.
The six shots that make up this panorama, captured by NASA’s Curiosity on Aug. 11, were stitched together after being sent back to Earth. Unlike most images from the rover’s Mastcam, this one was processed without the usual white balancing — an artistic choice that preserves the early morning appearance.
The yardang layer extends roughly 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. In fact, the rover recently passed another milestone in its ascent, reaching 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) of elevation — the most ever climbed on Mars. As it draws ever-closer to the yardangs, mission scientists expect to get even more amazing imagery — and, they hope, answers to how these cliffs were created.
Mount Sharp is made up of layers, each recording a distinct period of Mars’ history. By studying them, scientists have been able to learn more about lakes and streams that covered this part of the Red Planet billions of years ago. Eventually, the water dried up and left salty minerals behind. After new material stopped settling on the mountain, some of it may have been stripped away by wind, giving rise to the yardangs.
This artist’s concept shows Mount Sharp, the 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that NASA’s Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. The location of the yardang layer, which the rover recently captured from a distance, is indicated by an ellipse annotation on the mountain’s northwestern shoulder.
NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover captured this view looking back at the floor of Gale Crater on Sept. 5, 2026. Just nine days prior, the rover had marked 1 kilometer of elevation gain above the crater floor since beginning its ascent of Mount Sharp in 2014.
“The yardang layer looks out of place. It’s the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on,” said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “But that’s what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions.”
Curiosity is in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which started with an exploration of the spiderweb-like boxwork ridges . The rover will spend most of the next year or so driving through layers enriched with sulfates and carbonates, both signs of ancient drying on the surface. Sometime in 2027, scientists hope to reach the base of the yardangs, where Curiosity will be able to use its robotic arm to collect one-of-a-kind data on these mysterious features.

articles.title_orig: Moab wingsuiter overcomes serious injuries to reach World Championships
articles.title_zh: Moab wingsuiter overcomes serious injuries to reach World Championships
articles.content_orig:
( Joe Lohmuller) From the left, Clark Robinson, Joe Lohmuller and Alex Knaub won Nationals in 2025 and advanced to the World Championships.
Less than two years after an accident left him with a broken pelvis and sacrum, Moab wingsuit pilot Joe Lohmuller is heading to represent the United States on one of the sport’s biggest stages.
The 6th FAI World Wingsuit Flying Championships begin Oct. 8 at Skydive Elsinore in Lake Elsinore, California, bringing competitors from around the world together for a week of performance and acrobatic wingsuit flying.
For Lohmuller, the event is the culmination of more than a year spent almost singularly focused on getting there.
“I have had 13 and a half months of giving this my all with one focus,” Lohmuller said.
The push began under unlikely circumstances.
On April 5, 2025, Lohmuller was seriously injured in an accident that broke his pelvis and sacrum and severed his urethra. Twelve weeks later, on July 2, he was jumping again.
During his recovery, Lohmuller said he held onto something a doctor in Moab told him shortly after the accident: he would be back on his feet in about six weeks.
“It was one of the worst experiences ever,” Lohmuller said. But he focused on physical therapy and on how fortunate he had been to survive without more permanent injuries.
Then came a phone call from his friend and former teammate, Clark Robinson, asking whether Lohmuller wanted to compete again.
Despite needing another surgery, Lohmuller agreed. After recovering, he trained for about 10 days with Robinson before competing at the 2025 national championships. They won, earning a place on the U.S. Parachute Team and a path to the following year’s World Championships.
From there, training accelerated.
Lohmuller and Robinson spent weeks at a time jumping and training in horizontal wind tunnels, where wingsuit pilots can practice body positioning and maneuvers in a controlled environment.
(Courtesy photo) Alex Knaub, dark suit, films Joe Lohmuller and Clark Robinson at the 2025 National Championship.
During one three-week session, Lohmuller said the pair logged 18 hours and 25 minutes together in the tunnel — which he estimated was equivalent to more than 500 skydives. They continued training throughout the year, including another tunnel session in Slovenia this past summer.
In the final weeks before Worlds, Lohmuller planned to complete four or five jumps each day.
“Just trying to sharpen the ax,” he said.
Acrobatic wingsuit competition combines precision with choreography. Competitors complete compulsory rounds built around prescribed maneuvers and free rounds where teams develop their own routines.
Lohmuller compares the latter to pairs figure skating, with judges evaluating the quality of the flying, the routine and the camera flyer, who is also part of the team.
At nationals, Lohmuller said his team set a national record with 49 “docks,” or completed grips between flyers, surpassing the previous record of 37.
But executing those maneuvers requires more than individual skill.
Finding the right team, Lohmuller said, can be a “magic act,” requiring people with compatible skill, commitment, finances, schedules and personalities.
“Flying with someone is like dancing with someone,” he said. “There’s certain people you can do it really well with when you have chemistry together, and certain people you just can’t do it with.”
When that chemistry works, he said, it becomes something worth appreciating.
“There’s literally nothing more special than just having somebody that wants to fly with you,” Lohmuller said.
That perspective is informed in part by loss. Lohmuller has lost friends in the sport and these experiences have shaped the way he thinks about the people he flies with and the time they have together.
“You just learn to appreciate what you have when you have it,” he said. “You don’t see terrible things coming, but in my line of work, they happen from time to time.
“You have to just let it influence you in a good way of being appreciative and being positive, ” he added.
For all the speed involved, Lohmuller describes wingsuit flying in unexpectedly meditative terms.
“I just call it ‘fast yoga,’” he said. “You’re just trying to achieve the perfect body configuration … and it’s these tiny little movements that turn into what you’re doing.”
With the competition imminent and pressure mounting, Lohmuller said he is going to keep his approach simple.
“Eventually there is nothing left to prepare for. I’m just going to go out there, do my best and try and have some fun.”

articles.title_orig: Health officials report 74 new measles cases in Pennsylvania - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Health officials report 74 new measles cases in Pennsylvania - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Five people have died in the state so far this year.
Pennsylvania is reporting 74 new measles cases since Monday, the state's health department said Wednesday.
A total of 1,078 cases have been reported in the state so far this year. At least 207 people have been hospitalized and five people have died, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) .
"Of the 74 cases added, more than 40 represent individuals who were sick more than two weeks ago and are no longer contagious, but their cases were only recently reported and subsequently confirmed, the DOH said. Wednesday's update "does not reflect a current surge in new infections."
Of the five people who died, two of the deaths were among unvaccinated adults: an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old. The other two deaths were among infants who were too young to have received the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine.
The fifth death occurred in an unvaccinated resident of Lancaster County, in southeastern Pennsylvania, but it is unclear how old the individual is. Lancaster County is the epicenter of the state's outbreak, with 401 cases confirmed so far.
One-third of cases are among those under 18 years old and fewer than 1% of cases are among those fully vaccinated with the MMR shot, according to DOH data.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective in preventing measles infection and two doses are 97% effective, the CDC says.
Infants aged 6 to 11 months living in or traveling to high-risk outbreak areas may receive an early third dose of the MMR vaccine.
CDC data, however shows vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2025-26 school year, 92.4% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 95.2% seen in the 2019-20 school year, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic.
"State health center staff have administered more than 5,700 MMR vaccinations at 198 pop-up vaccination clinics in the affected communities since the outbreak began in late April," DOH wrote in a press release on Wednesday.
"Dozens of additional vaccine clinics are scheduled for the upcoming weeks and months, based on community interest and need," the press release continued. "In pop-up clinics and at state health centers combined, Department nurses have administered nearly 9,000 MMR vaccine doses to residents across the Commonwealth in 2026."

articles.title_orig: Hundreds of new pro sports team ETFs lead world of retail investing to the edge of gambling
articles.title_zh: Hundreds of new pro sports team ETFs lead world of retail investing to the edge of gambling
articles.content_orig:
In 1989, all-time hits leader Pete Rose was banned from Major League Baseball for life because of his gambling activities. He wasn't reinstated until last year, months after his death in 2024.
Fast-forward to today, and Pete Rose's gambling might seem like just another day on Wall Street as financial firms expand the ways fans can put money behind their teams, beyond a beer and a $15 hot dog.
You may soon be able to buy a ticker for your favorite hockey team, and it isn't a stake in the franchise. Multiple asset managers have filed to launch dozens of ETFs, one for every NHL team, with MLB baseball team funds filed as well, all built on new futures contracts that track a team's season statistics. None has begun trading but in all, hundreds of ETFs that track the single-season performance of one professional team across a mix of statistical categories have been filed at the SEC for approval.
Some finance experts see the development as lacking any nuance whatsoever.
"The line between gambling and investing has not simply been blurred, it has been erased," said Robert Johnson, a professor of finance at Creighton University.
Among fund companies getting in on the novel trend are VolatilityShares , LeagueShares, Roundhill Investments , and Rex Financial .
None of the four companies responded to requests for comment. Asset managers typically cannot publicly comment during the period between when funds are filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission for approval and when they become effective, if approved.
Rex, a Miami-based ETF issuer, announced Sept. 21 that it was launching Alpha Sports Holdings, a new subsidiary built to turn team performance into exchange-traded funds. REX has filed with the SEC for BaseballShares and HockeyShares, suites of ETFs that would track Major League Baseball and National Hockey League teams through futures contracts that CME Group, the derivatives exchange, lists on indexes built by FutureSports, an index company. The underlying CME futures , which began trading for NHL teams in late September, need to first establish a trading history.
Each team's index opens the season at a set number and moves as the team racks up statistics, including runs scored, stolen bases and strikeouts for baseball, then resets in the offseason.
"The sports industry generates hundreds of billions of dollars a year, but there has never been a liquid, transparent investment product tied directly to what happens in live games," said Greg King, CEO of Alpha Sports, in a press release. "Alpha Sports exists to build that product for passionate investors who want to participate in the fortunes of their favorite teams."
Johnson, though, said the sports-themed ETFs are far more gaming than investing.
"I thought that the ETF world had jumped the shark with the introduction of the 2X and 3X leveraged and inverse ETFs. In my mind these were simply vehicles for short term speculators. But, at least these vehicles were based upon assets. The new structures — and I call them structures, not assets — are simply gambling dressed up as investing," Johnson said.
In fact, the proposed team ETFs include in some cases leveraged versions of trades on single-team performance.
The boom in prediction markets is already blurring the lines between sports wagering and market trading, with regulatory battles intensifying over the distinction — CNBC reported on Thursday that the NFL is pushing for prediction markets to be regulated by state gambling authorities. Unlike prediction markets contracts, the sports team ETFs are tracking futures off an index rather than a single event (e.g. win or loss). But while structurally contracts in this market have a role to play for investors, in the case of sports performance, Johnson says the case is weak.
"They have societal value in that parties are able to hedge natural positions and transact with other speculators willing to bear that risk. This allows a more optimal allocation of risk," Johnson said.
But he added that is not the case when individual investors are making bets on the performance of sports teams they follow.
"There are no natural positions being hedged. In the aggregate, they destroy wealth," Johnson said.
Here's a look at other stories offering insight on ETFs for investors.
Alex Michalka, vice president of investment research at investing platform Wealthfront, said the case for investing in the performance of sports teams is nearly impossible to separate from gambling, since wagering on whether a sports team will win or lose does not facilitate an economic purpose that adds value to the world.
"That is not to say a legitimate economic use case is impossible, but most people will likely use these funds for the same reasons they place a sports bet, which is often to show loyalty to a team or simply for entertainment," Michalka said. "Just because sports betting has an ETF wrapper, it does not change the risk associated with it," Michalka added.
Futures have long been used for hedging, and the CME contracts and FutureSports may be ways for sponsors, broadcasters, insurers and arena vendors to potentially hedge exposure against assets and liabilities. Conceptually, that's similar to an airline hedging fuel prices or an insurer hedging extreme weather risks. But in actuality, that does not apply to the vast majority of investors when it comes to these specific sports investments.
"Sports as an asset class exists, but for a few very select people out there," said Todd Sohn, chief ETF strategist at Baird Strategas. "I'm unsure if 'democratizing' really makes sense here," he said.
He added there are also many risks when it comes to novel ETFs like these with so few buyers in the market with a justifiable economic reason to trade them, risks that range from liquidity to price discovery and manipulation. Insider trading around injuries, trades, and coaching changes; and illiquidity in the investments during the offseason, up to four months of no activity, though trades and free agency can impact outlook, are among them. There should also be the expectations for wide bid/ask spreads and market imbalances with "fan enthusiasm driving prices and no commercial hedgers," Baird Strategas wrote in a preliminary analysis.
Despite the risks, all of which are covered in risk disclosures within these ETFs' prospectuses, Nate Geraci, an ETF expert and president of NovaDius Wealth Management, expects them to be approved by the SEC. Assuming the futures contracts "function properly, and establish sufficient liquidity, I don't see a regulatory reason why the SEC wouldn't approve the ETFs. CME-traded futures held in an ETF wrapper certainly aren't novel, though it's entirely possible the SEC could attempt to classify these sports-focused ETFs as such," he said.
The SEC is currently in the midst of a rulemaking proposal and public comment period covering "novel" ETFs, a move the regulator made after ETF companies filed for prediction markets ETFs.
Geraci is not surprised that ETF issuers are chasing the concept. "It's somewhat ironic that ETFs began as a way to offer low-cost, broad-based exposure to the market and have morphed in recent years into expensive, narrowly focused speculation vehicles. That said, it's a tale as old as time in asset management, where fund issuers rush to package and sell whatever is capturing investors' attention," he said.
Evan Mills, a financial advisor at Scholar Advising, an independent fee-only advisory firm, said it is important to understand the difference between owning a productive asset and making a bet on an outcome.
"If you're buying stock in a business, that stock is tied to revenue, earnings, and cash flow, so it appreciates based on that, as well as demand for the stock," Mills said. Bonds, meanwhile, include a contractual stream of payments, and that's how you make money off them.

articles.title_zh: South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute
articles.content_orig:
FILE - Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters, on Sept. 23, 2026. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption
SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea said Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, stepping up its protest against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recent revelation of a supposedly secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
The South Korean announcement came days after its President Lee Jae Myung threatened to take unspecified punitive steps if Ukraine refuses to apologize over the revelation.
South Korea's Foreign Ministry didn't say when the ambassador, Park Hee-chang, will be brought back home. A ministry statement said that South Korea will continue consultations with Ukraine, adding it hopes the dispute between the two countries would be resolved smoothly.
South Korea and Ukraine became embroiled in a diplomatic row after Zelenskyy spoke about the transfer of the North Korean soldiers during his U.N. speech on Sept. 23. South Korea has accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement on their transfer in mid-September, but Kyiv has denied agreeing to such a deal.
The soldiers were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia's war against Ukraine. Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers had expressed their desires to resettle in South Korea, because they could face persecution if repatriated home. South Korea had said it would accept them, because it legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.
South Korean officials said the non-disclosure agreement was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North. But many experts say South Korea's liberal government likely also worries the disclosure of their arrival may hurt its efforts to improve ties with North Korea.
North Korea's state media hasn't commented on the soldiers' transfer. But the North previously reacted with fury to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them. North Korea has shunned any talks with South Korea and the U.S. and focused on bolstering its nuclear program since 2019.
It's unclear what other steps South Korea would take. Experts say maintaining good relations with Ukraine is in South Korean national interests because Kyiv could provide Seoul with intelligence about North Korea's expanding cooperation with Russia and its battlefield experiences. They say cooperation with Ukraine is important for South Korea's partnerships with many Western countries supporting Ukraine over the war.
Observers say Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of the North Korean POWs to expose the danger of North Korea's military support to Russia as a way to win more international assistance.
South Korea has provided $445 million in humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since 2022. In July, Lee pledged $100 million in aid to Ukraine in a meeting with Zelenskyy,

This episode maps the early weeks of oral zongertinib and the real-world factors that threaten them.
This episode maps the early weeks of oral zongertinib and the real-world factors that threaten them. The panel describes a model in which a clinical pharmacist calls the patient at home to confirm the drug has arrived and review administration, followed by an early advanced practice provider visit with labs, a second visit shortly after, and body imaging within the first few months. Faculty explain how community practices without an embedded thoracic pharmacist can replicate this through pharmacotherapy referrals, virtual visits, and phone outreach, and how pharmacists catch dosing nuances such as weight-based dosing and drug interactions. The discussion then examines why patients stop therapy outside trials, from distance and transportation barriers to unprepared reactions to low-grade diarrhea, and dispels the idea that dose reduction sacrifices efficacy. The episode closes on fragmented community care, where the time from diagnosis to drug in hand can stretch past a month.

articles.title_orig: Cornell defendant is fighting AG Letitia James’ appointment as special prosecutor
articles.title_zh: Cornell defendant is fighting AG Letitia James’ appointment as special prosecutor
articles.content_orig:
One of the seven men named in the lawsuit filed by a former Cornell University student who alleges that she was sexually assaulted at an on-campus fraternity house has filed a petition to block New York Attorney General Letitia James’ appointment as special prosecutor in the case .
The attorney for Gillio Lopes, who has denied that he sexually assaulted the woman, filed a petition in Albany County Supreme Court on Wednesday. His filing says James should not be the prosecutor in the case because she has “unequivocally demonstrated a bias and presumption of guilt against the defendants named in the Civil Case.”
The Article 78 petition, filed against James and Gov. Kathy Hochul, is a proceeding used to challenge an action by a state or local government officer or agencies in New York.
Hochul appointed James last week to independently investigate Jane Doe’s allegations in the lawsuit, in which she says she was plied with alcohol, sexually assaulted and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. In her role, James will determine whether criminal charges are warranted.
James’ office declined to comment on the Article 78 filing.
In a statement Monday, James said: “My office enforces our state’s laws to protect all New Yorkers. I am committed to leading a comprehensive investigation they can trust, guided only by the facts, the evidence, and the law.”
Hochul’s office reiterated support for James on Wednesday.
Reached for comment on Lopes’ filing, the governor’s office referred to her comments last week.
“I have every confidence in our Attorney General to do what she has always done: look at the facts, examine the record and draw the proper conclusions. That’s exactly what’s going to happen in this case,” Hochul said at the time.
Hochul appointed James after she expressed dismay over Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten’s investigation of Doe’s allegations. He has said his office found a lack of criminality at the time and declined to press charges, but he reopened the case after the lawsuit sparked national uproar.
Jane Doe’s civil suit was filed last month against Cornell, Chi Phi and seven fraternity brothers. None of the men named have been criminally charged.
The fraternity was suspended from campus, and it remains barred.
Cornell said in a statement Sept. 28 that it conducted a thorough, monthslong Title IX investigation in 2024 that handed down “a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions ” from the university. Two of the fraternity members were expelled, and two others were suspended. A third, who had already graduated, was barred from campus, and the final two were issued no-contact orders and required to write “reflection papers,” according to a source who has seen the written decision of the Title IX investigation.
Lopes’ filing argues that James’ appointment is “improper” and cites a post her office shared on X on Sept. 28 , three days before her appointment was announced. In the post, she said: “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.”
The post, the petition contends, “made clear that she has formed an opinion about the case” and that “she has already reached the conclusion that Petitioner and the other named Defendants are guilty.”
The petition also seeks to have the court review James’ appointment and asks that her appointment be annulled or modified so she is not personally directing the probe or any resulting prosecution.
Stuart Bernstein, an attorney for Lopes, said Wednesday: “As Governor Hochul has said, the public needs confidence in the individual leading this investigation. AG James, based upon her very public statements validating Jane Doe, certainly doesn’t instill confidence in a fair investigation.”
In her lawsuit, Doe accuses Lopes of kissing her and sexually assaulting her without her consent.
Attorneys for two of the seven men, including Lopes, have denied to NBC News that they sexually assaulted Doe. An attorney for a third man denied the allegations to ABC News. NBC News has not received responses to requests for comment from the other men.
On Tuesday, Andrew Miltenberg, an attorney for Lopes, said he welcomes Cornell’s decision to have an independent review of its handling of Doe’s allegations, which will be led by former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates.
“In our experience, Cornell’s investigations have generally been thorough. That said, we have also seen due process problems that have affected respondents, and on at least two occasions we have gone to federal court to try to address those issues. In this case, we do not agree with the outcome as to Mr. Lopes,” Miltenberg said.

articles.title_orig: The World is His Oyster
articles.title_zh: The World is His Oyster
articles.content_orig:
October 8, 2026 | Claire Hall
Seafood entrepreneur Keegan Jalbert is developing a new approach to oyster feed
Graduate student Keegan Jalbert, left, and his brother-in-law Bryan Zambrano are pictured on a boat as they visit an aquaculture farm in Ecuador, where they discussed feed trials using AccessFlora's proprietary omega-3 feed. Jalbert's startup is one of the finalists in next week's Wolff New Venture Competition (UConn Today).
Graduate student Keegan Jalbert ’23 (CLAS) ’27 MS has always been interested in agriculture, food, and innovation. Today he is finding new ways to grow oysters and share his love of seafood with customers who live far from the ocean.
Jalbert is the founder of AccessFlora , a sustainable aquaculture company with a proprietary omega-3 aquafeed for raising oysters in purified water at a hatchery. The outcome is a larger and healthier shellfish that isn’t confined to the coast nor dependent upon favorable ocean conditions.
“I think what keeps me going as an entrepreneur is that this work is very fun,’’ says Jalbert, who is pursuing a master’s degree in nutritional science. “My greatest motivation is the impact on how we source omega-3s as a critical nutrient for our human health and for agriculture. What’s helped me so much with the startup is that I love my work, and because of it I’ve developed great personal connections.’’
Startup to Compete in Wolff New Venture Championship
AccessFlora is one of five UConn-affiliated startups participating in the Wolff New Venture Competition next Tuesday, Oct. 13, at Pratt & Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field in East Hartford.
The competition, now in its 11th year, is hosted by the Connecticut Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation (CCEI) . The event will include awards of more than $150,000, including a $40,000 grand prize for the first-place finisher. Jalbert says whatever money AccessFlora wins will help ramp up production.
“In terms of shellfish farming, yes, what we’re doing is revolutionary,’’ Jalbert says. “Shellfish are not raised in land-based aquaculture because the omega-3 feed would be too expensive. On one hand, that makes shellfish really great, because they can grow out in the ocean without being fed and they are great for the environment. But on the other hand, this cultivation method takes a long time, it is labor intensive, and it is vulnerable to unpredictable ocean conditions. While our technology will not replace traditional shellfish farming, it does provide a highly resilient and quick way to raise oysters, independent of ocean access, allowing this to be done inland.’’
“The way that this technology works is that we have a healthy microalgae that we use to convert vinegar into omega-3 in controlled conditions, kind of like yeast turns sugars into alcohol,’’ Jalbert says. “This gives us a clean DHA omega-3, the nutrient that makes seafood such an important part in our diet.’’
But that’s just one step for the company.
“Our longer-term plan is for this to not just be raising oysters, but to be serving as an omega-3 source in enriched/fortified plant-based foods,’’ Jalbert says. “This is because that is a large market that our technology is really well suited for, especially now that the majority of U.S. population is deficient in omega-3.’’
Jalbert Brings Extensive Experience to His Work
Jalbert’s startup won the 2025 Innovation Quest competition at UConn and a $15,000 grand prize. He has partnered with professor Mingyu Qiao, in the Department of Nutritional Sciences in the College of Agriculture, Health and Natural Resources, who is a leader and innovator in sustainable food systems.
In addition, Jalbert took advantage of UConn’s co-op program and worked with both the Boston Beer Company, in new product development, and as a microbiology intern at the U.S. Department of Energy. Through exchange programs, he has learned about shellfish aquaculture in Melbourne, Australia, Manabi, Ecuador, as well as here in Connecticut.
Summer Accelerator: ‘I Must Have Learned 100 Things’
Part of Jalbert’s entrepreneurial journey included attending CCEI’s eight-week Summer Accelerator, which offers promising startups $15,000 in non-dilutive funding, mentorship, access to masterclasses and workshops, and pro-bono legal, accounting, marketing, product development, and banking services.
“Summer Accelerator is like a summer camp for startups,’’ Jalbert says. “It packs a lot into eight weeks. This summer we were testing how we can distribute our omega-3 product and learning the cost structures and economics of getting product to customers. I must have learned 100 things during Summer Accelerator, but the biggest thing was unit economics and cost structure of bringing the product to market.’’
With the oyster feed gaining traction, AccessFlora is focusing on educating people on the seafood nutrient. Jalbert just hired his first employee to work on business outreach. “We are in real talks with restaurants and agricultural experts,’’ he says.
AccessFlora also manages a food trailer, called Reef-to-Table, which caters weddings and other events. Although that isn’t the primary focus of the business, it is a terrific outlet for Jalbert.
“It’s a good way of having direct interactions with consumers. I enjoy it so much,’’ he says. “I have to be conscience of my time commitments, but if it could be my weekend hobby, I’d do it. The raw bar business is a ton of fun and already profitable.”
The Wolff New Venture Competition will be held on Tuesday (Oct. 13) at Pratt and Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field in East Hartford from 5 to 9 p.m. The event is free to attend and all are welcome. Pre-registration is required at https://luma.com/i2690pqa .

articles.title_orig: Alabama’s Prehistoric Past: Fossils Reveal a World That Existed Millions of Years Ago
articles.title_zh: Alabama’s Prehistoric Past: Fossils Reveal a World That Existed Millions of Years Ago
articles.content_orig:
by Brian White, Ashonti Ford
When most people think about dinosaur fossils, they may picture the wide-open landscapes of Montana, Wyoming or the Dakotas.
But some of the most significant fossil discoveries in the country are much closer to home — right here in Alabama.
Inside the Birmingham Mcwane Center, thousands of fossils are stored just feet away from visitors, offering a glimpse into an Alabama that existed long before the state — or even humans — were here.
Behind collection-room doors, row after row of cabinets hold bones, teeth and other remnants of life dating back more than half a billion years.
June Ebersole, director of collections at McWane Science Center, oversees about half a million specimens, including fossils found nowhere else in the world.
“A lot of people think you have to go out west to find fossils,” Ebersole said. “But what my research is showing is that Alabama, by far, is the number one state in the U.S. in terms of paleo-biodiversity.”
The collection spans an extraordinary stretch of time.
“We have fossils here that are over 500 million years old, to some that are just from the Ice Age, only 12,000 to 14,000 years old, and everything in between,” Ebersole said. “We have so many fossils here, I’m discovering new species all the time.”
Among the most remarkable specimens is one that helped change what scientists knew about dinosaurs in the eastern United States.
Ebersole opens a drawer containing the remains of Eotrachodon orientalis, a newly identified species of duck-billed dinosaur.
The fossils may look like a pile of bones to the untrained eye, but together they represent the most complete dinosaur ever found in the eastern half of the United States, with about 60% of its skeleton recovered.
And the discovery was made not in a remote western desert, but in Montgomery County.
“It’s from Montgomery County, right on the side of the creek, just outside the city limits,” Ebersole said. “This is the only one of this particular species in the world.”
The dinosaur is only part of Alabama’s prehistoric story.
The McWane collection also includes fossils of sharks, turtles and birds, along with a 315-million-year-old dragonfly wing discovered in Walker County.
Thousands of fossil shark teeth fill drawers inside the collection, including one massive collection from the time of the dinosaurs.
“It is literally — here’s 10,000 fossil goblin shark teeth,” Ebersole said. “It’s one of the biggest collections of these on the planet.”
Most visitors to the science center will see only a fraction of the collection.
But behind the scenes, scientists continue studying the specimens and making discoveries that help reconstruct the world that existed beneath Alabama millions of years ago.
Long before 250 years of American history, Alabama was already writing a story of its own — one measured not in centuries, but in hundreds of millions of years.
And today, pieces of that ancient story remain carefully preserved, waiting to reveal what Alabama looked like long before any of us arrived.

articles.title_orig: Top Climate Scientists Set Out Five Steps to Help the World Prepare for Super El NiñO | Newswise
articles.title_zh: Top Climate Scientists Set Out Five Steps to Help the World Prepare for Super El NiñO | Newswise
articles.content_orig:
Newswise — Researchers have identified five key ways countries across the globe can be better prepared for the impending El Niño – and reduce its potentially devastating toll on human health.
The call to action , led by the University of Bristol and published in The Lancet , highlights how although it is widely-acknowledged El Niño exacerbates wide-ranging health risks posed by climate change, the additional threats presented remain largely unquantified. The researchers emphasise that as the El Niño cycle can be forecasted months in advance, preparatory measures should be put in place to mitigate the impact, especially in countries most vulnerable.
Study lead author Dr Ruby Lieber, Senior Research Associate in Climate Science at the University of Bristol, said: “We know the number of people affected by climate-related disasters is strongly influenced by the El Niño cycle, but there is little evidence available establishing how much of the health burden can be attributed to climate change and how much was driven by El Niño.
“Since the current El Niño pushes many regions into more extreme climates, there’s a pressing and unprecedented need to better understand, measure and pinpoint the different dangers for individual countries and places.”
The study recommends five important actions to gain this comprehensive risk overview, which holds the key to being able to tackle and minimise the likely consequences, including the spread of infectious diseases, malnutrition, and various heat-related conditions such as dehydration and heatstroke.
Dr Lieber said: “These steps will require greater collaboration between climate and health researchers and, equally fundamental, concerted action between research funders, the World Health Organization (WHO), the wider UN system, the World Bank, and non-governmental organisations.
“Partnership working is imperative and such global entities need to urgently call on advances in attribution science to more accurately recognise and assess how much of the repercussions are the result of human-induced climate change and how much are a result of El Niño. By isolating the El Niño-related impacts, we can generate much more targeted and event-specific actions.”
A significant El Niño, which describes the warming of sea surface temperature, is likely to occur towards the end of this year with some forecasts predicting the strongest event on record. The direct effects of El Niño will be felt across the globe and may heighten instances of extreme weather in regions such as India, East Asia, South America, parts of Africa and the West Pacific.
Co-author Dann Mitchell, Shanta Professorial Chair in Planetary Health at the University of Bristol, added: “It’s clear that we cannot afford to ignore this emerging threat, which poses potentially devastating but predictable risks to communities around the world.
“Climate and health researchers must unite, with the full backing of national and international agencies, to create a much more advanced evidence base. This will enable us to ramp up global resilience and implement adaptation strategies to mitigate the many deeply concerning health implications, particularly for countries more acutely exposed.”

COLUMBIA, Md. , Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Following the biennial gathering of the world's fire leaders at the World Fire Congress, UL Research Institutes' Fire Safety Research Institute is powering the ongoing Communities of Practice (CoPs) to advance solutions for the most pressing global fire safety issues. "The inaugural World Fire Congress and Communities of Practice in 2024 established the foundation for sustained and collaborative knowledge exchange, and ULRI is honored to build on that foundation," said Dr. Lori Moore-Merrell, World Fire Congress founder and chief fire safety strategist for the Fire Safety Research Institute. "Drawing on more than a century of fire research and leadership, ULRI is bringing its scientific rigor into the global conversation, ensuring the dialogue is grounded in evidence over anecdote."
The World Fire Congress CoPs offer the fire service a mechanism to share knowledge, align on emerging risks and translate research and training into practice across borders. Through ULRI, members gain access to a trusted international network, curated best practices and direct engagement with leading researchers and their work on areas including lithium-ion battery safety, EV fire risk, climate adaptation and evidence-based tactical decision-making. Each CoP will be equipped with the necessary infrastructure to collaborate across nations and will be grounded with an Anchor Organization to bring established expertise and leadership to each Community.

In collaboration with ULRI's Fire Safety Research Institute, ULSE supports monthly meetings, research analysis, and reports for CoPs members.

The inaugural World Fire Congress was held in Washington D.C. in 2024. articles.title_orig: He planned to become a philosopher. Then he found New Orleans’ startup world.
articles.title_zh: He planned to become a philosopher. Then he found New Orleans’ startup world.
articles.content_orig:
In college, Andrew Albert imagined a career in academia. He’d get global experience, earn a PhD in philosophy, come back to start a think tank in New Orleans and shape public policy in his hometown.
In the end, he did build a career that contributes to New Orleans — but in the city’s startup ecosystem.
He’s now programs director at the Idea Village , where he leads the team responsible for its accelerators, thought leadership and marketing and communications.
“What does it mean to be Black in the South and wrestle with institutions and power?”
His path there included working at New Orleans software startup Lucid during its $60 million Series B, before it became New Orleans’ first tech unicorn. He went on to support founders through Venture for America , co-found River Basin Distillery and later launch Exclave Spirits .
In this edition of How I Got Here , Albert talked about trading academia for startups, the job he considers his “working MBA” and what people hoping to build companies should know.
This Q&A has been edited for length and clarity.
Being Black from New Orleans, it was like: Go be a lawyer, go be a doctor. Those are the traditional pathways. So I started my undergrad career at Loyola University New Orleans as a bio major. I was like, “Oh, cool. I guess I’ll go become a doctor.”
But because Loyola is a Jesuit university, all freshmen take Intro to Philosophy. I had a chem lab with no windows and fluorescent lights, and then I went to this philosophy class with these very heady questions. It was incredibly appealing.
I literally dropped everything within that semester and switched to philosophy.
A lot of my undergraduate career was spent studying dynamics of power, specifically racial power. What does it mean to be Black in the South and wrestle with institutions and power? How might you see yourself in the world?
I had every intention of being a full-time academic. I had an amazing mentor who suggested I get a master’s degree first to figure out whether grad school was really what I wanted.
I’d had a Fulbright experience in the UK and fell in love with London. I was also a super nerd. You hear the stories about James Baldwin and the intellectual expat, and I knew I wanted to do something abroad.
So I went to the London School of Economics to study philosophy and public policy.
I immediately got to grad school and was like, “I do not like this at all.”
Before that, my ambition was to get a PhD, make policy recommendations, yada yada yada, solve the world’s problems. That was my very naive educational journey.
I knew fairly quickly that my educational journey was going to stop at the master’s level. In retrospect, that was probably a great thing because it gave me time to reflect on what I actually wanted to do.
A core driver for me was: How might I participate within the city of New Orleans in some productive fashion? Originally, I thought it was policy. I realized I didn’t want to do that.
This was the golden age of startups, and I was living in East London, where there was a lot of buzz and excitement around them.
One option was Venture for America, a fellowship for recent grads who wanted to work at high-growth startups. I applied, got accepted and really put all my eggs in the “I’m working in New Orleans” basket.
Thinking back on it, I had this singular idea: Whatever the best company in the world is, that’s the company I’m going to work for.
Plan B was to do Plan A for me.
I was fortunate enough to land that role at Lucid.
My title was executive analyst, but I worked there essentially in a chief of staff role. I did everything from financial planning and analysis and board governance to designing a 35,000-sq.-ft.office space. If there was a job that needed to be done and there wasn’t a full-time hire to do it, it was my role.
My time at Lucid was very much my working MBA. We raised a $60 million Series B, which in New Orleans was a massive amount of capital. I got to work with bankers.
I remember the CEO at the time telling me, “The amount of access that you’re going to get here far surpasses what you’re supposed to have, and it is going to completely warp how you move through your profession.”
Then I pivoted away from operationally working in startups and went back to what I was interested in from school: economic development.
I ended up working for Venture for America. First, I was director of New Orleans, and then I became VP of venture growth, where I spent most of my time building our venture growth department, essentially the entrepreneurship department.
I helped design how we supported fellows and alumni on their entrepreneurial journeys, ran our accelerator and all of our entrepreneurial programming. It really was like 1-800-founder for the better part of six and a half years.
Around 2017 or 2018, I read the story of Nearest Green and Uncle Nearest Whiskey. I remember thinking, “God damn, why didn’t I come up with this? This is amazing.”
After those emotions went away, the next thing was: This is actually a global Black story that can and should be told. This isn’t just an American Black story.
That seed eventually became part of Exclave Spirits, which tells a broader story of how Black people have contributed to distilled spirits.
Actually building something changed how I work with founders. It’s the difference between theory and practice.
By building something, I was able to cut out the jargon and get to the foundational principles of what it means to build a business.
The hard part is being able to assess risk, anticipate things and make very tight resource decisions. You hear stories of investors pushing, pushing, pushing, and founders losing sight of why they got into it in the first place.
My approach is: I don’t know exactly what you’re going through. This shit is hard. It’s lonely. It’s winding. But I try to be the friendly voice saying, “All right, I know it’s hard, but keep pushing.”
Being perpetually curious is something you can develop and always work on.
Be comfortable with pivoting, because everything we put on a whiteboard sounds great to ourselves. The minute you take a step forward, you’re going to face something that forces you to change.
There’s the “fail fast” adage. I switch it to: Be able to pivot and rebound fast.
The other thing is to be very diligent with how you question your customers. You can build something great, something technologically ahead of everybody else. Awesome. But what I always go back to is: Will somebody give you money for it repeatedly?
If not, you kind of just have a science project, which is cool. But at the core of it, a business is: You create value that somebody pays you for.
And what’s the worst that could happen?
The cost of building is as low as it’s probably ever been. To the extent that you see a problem, see a challenge, take a shot. What’s the worst thing that’s going to happen?

articles.title_orig: A Vail mountaineer is vying to be the first American woman to scale the world's tallest volcanoes
articles.title_zh: A Vail mountaineer is vying to be the first American woman to scale the world's tallest volcanoes
articles.content_orig:
In August 2024, Vail’s Nicole Otake climbed Papua New Guinea’s Mount Giluwe, the highest volcano in Oceania.
Getting there required the kind of logistics that adventurous travelers love: “A guy picked us up at the airport, then handed us off to another guy and his son who connected us to someone else,” Otake said.
This story first appeared in The Outsider , the premium outdoor newsletter by Jason Blevins. In it, he covers the industry from the inside out, plus the fun side of being outdoors in our beautiful state.
Eventually, Otake and her climbing partner were led to a few men on the side of a road in Papua New Guinea’s Western Highlands where they all began a two-day trek toward the mountain. The men were barefoot and carried handmade spears.
Giluwe rises 14,327 feet — not especially high by mountaineering standards — but the climb was muddy, wet and remote. Along the way, Otake saw enormous prehistoric-looking birds running through the highlands.
“It was like being back in time,” Otake said. “It was super remote and super cool.”
It was also the fourth stop on a checklist: climbing the Seven Volcanic Summits, the highest volcanoes on each continent.
Otake, 32, has so far summited six of the seven. All that remains is Mount Sidley in Antarctica, the most remote of the seven and by far the most expensive to reach. If Otake gets there, she will become the first American woman to complete the Seven Volcanic Summits.
Otake started climbing mountains because she liked the idea of a challenge she could quantify. She is analytical and she likes spreadsheets and lists. The Seven Volcanic Summits gave her all three — along with a reason to start learning how to climb increasingly big and remote mountains.
Then, the mountains started leading her somewhere she hadn’t expected. From one summit, she would look across a valley and see another peak — one that wasn’t on any list, wasn’t particularly well known and, in some cases, was rarely climbed.
“Now there are so many mountains that aren’t on any of these lists that are so much higher on my list,” she said.
That shift — from checking off summits to seeking out remote mountains for their own sake — has also changed the way Otake thinks about mountaineering. She has learned how expensive and complicated mountaineering can be, and how much knowledge it takes to get into the mountains without paying someone else to handle everything. She has also learned that the sport is still overwhelmingly male and that many aspiring climbers, particularly women, lack the mentorship and resources she wished she had.
So this year, after losing the remote leadership job that had helped finance her climbing, Otake started Ash to Altitude, a small logistics company designed to help people plan their own expeditions — without the luxury price tag.
“I really believe people need access to these mountains,” she said.
Otake’s first big mountain — also one of the Seven Volcanic Summits — was Kilimanjaro, which she climbed in March 2023 in less than three days.
She had always been interested in volcanoes. Her father was born in Hawaii before it became a state , and because of that Otake grew up with a connection to the islands and the volcanoes that shape them. As she learned more about volcanoes around the world, she came across the Seven Volcanic Summits.
Learning that no American woman had completed the seven gave her new motivation.
“Someone will always be stronger or faster,” Otake said. “But you can’t take away the first of something.”
At first, the goal was simply to complete the list. But as Otake and her husband, Rocco, planned and executed the expeditions, they got hooked on going higher and farther. Rocco was also interested in climbing the traditional Seven Summits, the highest mountain on each continent, and the two began taking on bigger objectives together. In the process, Otake became the person handling the logistics.
“It lets my spreadsheet brain be happy,” she said.
The more mountains they climbed — like Denali and Mount Elbrus and Pico de Orizaba — the more the list became a gateway into alpine climbing. Each expedition taught them something about planning, logistics and what they were capable of taking on next. Ticking boxes became less and less important.
“Starting with a list has given us the skills and tools to become better mountaineers,” Otake said. “It was a good way to start because I wasn’t sure of anything else. But now there are so many mountains that aren’t on any of these lists that are so much more intriguing.”
Like Alpamayo in Peru, which she calls the most beautiful mountain in the world.
Even that experience, Otake said, made her want to look beyond the mountain she was climbing.
“But as we’re climbing that, it’s like, look across the valley and there’s Artesonraju , which is even more beautiful,” she said. “So now we’re going back next June.”
That curiosity has pushed Otake toward increasingly remote and self-supported objectives. She and Rocco have learned how to arrange their own transportation, permits, lodging, food and acclimatization rather than simply signing up for a commercial expedition and showing up at the trailhead.
Otake likes that part almost as much as the climbing.
She and Rocco live full time in a solar-powered van, spending much of the winter in the Vail Valley and leaving in the summer to climb. The van is minimalist: Otake says she owns one dress and one pair of heels, which both live crammed into a wheel well, while the couple’s climbing and skiing gear occupies the remaining space.
The setup suits a life organized around mountains. When she’s not climbing, Otake is usually planning the next climb — researching routes, comparing costs, figuring out transportation and finding people on the ground who can help them navigate places they have never been.
The process has given Otake a crash course in the barriers to mountaineering — not just the physical ones, but the financial and logistical ones, too. She has learned how much it costs to get to these places, how difficult it can be to know whom to trust and how much easier the process becomes if someone else has already figured it out.
The more time she spent in the mountains, the more Otake also noticed how difficult it can be for someone else to get started. Mountaineering is expensive. There is the gear, the international travel, the time required for training and acclimatization, and, for many mountains, thousands of dollars paid to an expedition company to arrange the logistics and guide the climb.
Otake had been fortunate. For four and a half years, she worked in leadership at Act Blue, a digital fundraising platform that builds open-access software for Democratic campaigns, progressive organizations, and 501(c)(3) organizations. The remote role allowed her to take extended time away for climbing. She bought her van and most of her equipment and learned how to organize increasingly complicated expeditions herself. “I was really lucky,” she said.
So, when Otake lost that job in May of 2025, she decided to try her hand at professionalizing something she already knew how to do.
In February, she started Ash to Altitude, a small expedition-planning company that helps climbers arrange their own trips. The idea is to work directly with local operators and strip away the overhead of a fully packaged expedition. Because Otake has already done so many expeditions herself, she knows how much they can cost — versus how much is often charged. She said she has seen companies charge about $7,000 for an Elbrus expedition that she can organize for roughly $3,000, including flights and a visa.
“It drives me crazy to see people exploit other people, especially to go to parts of the world where they can’t promote local pricing,” she says.

articles.title_zh: Flu season didn’t start when or where it was expected. Get your shot now, health officials say
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
This year’s flu season started months early and in an unexpected part of the country, according to health officials.
The unusually early start to the season has prompted local health officials to urge people to get their flu shots as soon as possible.
In Los Angeles County, flu activity began rising in September, ahead of its typical early-November start, Dr. Dawn Terashita told The Times on Wednesday.
That isn’t a major surprise, said Terashita, associate director of the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health’s Acute Communicable Disease Control Program. Flu tends to be “very unpredictable,” she said, due to the ways that it mutates.
But another unusual factor was that the flu season started this year in the Western states.
Typically, the flu starts in the South and Southeast, Dr. Helen Chu of the University of Washington School of Medicine told Huffpost . The disease “then sort of migrates up and then west,” Chu said, so the West Coast tends to get the flu last.
Terashita said it’s too soon to know the reason behind this phenomenon.
The county’s flu season started on Sept. 28. But the early start alone, she said, isn’t an indicator that the season will be more severe, she said.
The rate at which flu tests are coming back positive since the season’s start has been high in the San Francisco Bay Area and moderate in Southern California and the Sacramento Valley. Flu hospital admission rates remain low across California. So far this year, there have been 34 flu-related deaths in the state, according to the state Department of Public Health’s online dashboard .
San Francisco confirmed its first flu death of the season last week . Los Angeles County has not logged any influenza deaths yet this season, Terashita said. In the 2025-26 flu season, the county recorded 126 influenza deaths, a relatively low total, she noted.
Health officials say vaccination is the best form of protection against the flu and are urging people to get their shots soon.
Dr. Peter Chin-Hong, a UC San Francisco infectious-disease expert, said people should aim to get the shot ideally before mid-October. For most, he said, the standard flu shot suffices, though he noted there are other options, including a nasal spray version — great for almost anyone with a fear of needles — and higher-dosage shots. The stronger shots have four times the antigen and are approved for those 65 and older.
The current variant, H3N2 subclade K, appears similar to last year’s strain and is included in this year’s vaccine, reducing concern about a major mismatch between the vaccine and the flu strain, Chin-Hong said.
“The ball is in our court because vaccination behavior drives how we tackle the flu,” he said. “This year we have less excuse because the flu vaccine is well-matched in general to ... what has been circulating so far.”
Los Angeles County’s most severe flu season in recent memory was the 2009 pandemic, according to Terashita. That year, the H1N1 virus led to a high number of hospitalizations and deaths around the world, The Times reported at the time.
Flu cases almost disappeared during the COVID-19 pandemic, Terashita said. As people resumed gatherings and eased up on measures including masking and social distancing, the county saw upticks in flu cases in 2024 and 2025.
“We’re just watching and waiting right now” to see how severe the flu season will be, she said, “but it is a good reminder to everyone that it’s a very good thing you can do to protect yourself, which is get the vaccine.”
Times staff writer Rong-Gong Lin contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Gruesome injuries throw spotlight on France’s policing of high school protests
articles.title_zh: Gruesome injuries throw spotlight on France’s policing of high school protests
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — The police tear gas grenade shattered the 14-year-old’s jaw and many of his teeth. The officer who fired it was taken into custody a week later and charged with violent mutilation, punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Following surgery, the boy cannot speak and can only eat with a straw, his mother says.
Other adolescents have also suffered life-changing injuries blamed on police weaponry during nationwide protests by high school students demanding more funding for run-down schools. In the former mining town of Lens, a 15-year-old lost a hand in an incident involving a police stun grenade. In Tours, in the wine-making Loire region, the prosecutor there says a police riot-control round is suspected in the partial blinding of a 16-year-old.
Beyond physical wounds, the massive use of police arrests and tactics that government critics and human rights campaigners allege have been unnecessarily violent is giving a generation of French schoolchildren — and soon-to-be voters — a real-life education about state power and their rights as citizens, and how the two sometimes clash.
“It politicizes you at an incredible speed,” said Alexis Baudelin, a Paris attorney for more than a dozen youngsters taken into custody.
“For many of them — for all of them — this was one of the first times that they’d taken part in a demonstration, coming together in a public space to voice demands they considered legitimate.”
Police have swept up thousands of young people
According to the Interior Ministry, police have made more than 6,600 arrests — mostly of people under 18 — since protests began snowballing last week, including 488 people detained during nationwide demonstrations Tuesday. The movement demanding increased funds and more replacement teachers for schools started in a Paris-region high school in mid-September.
Lawyers and researchers who study French policing caution that the muscular response could spawn disillusioned young adults soured on the Republic and its promises of “ Liberty, Equality, Fraternity. “Police have been less forgiving with teenage protesters than they previously were when farmers, a powerful lobby in France, doused government buildings with manure, blocked roads and set fires.
Baudelin, the lawyer, said his young clients have had a crash course in “unrestrained violence from the police.”
“Being locked up for hours and hours with nothing, in cells that are for the most part extremely unsanitary, in police stations that smell terrible, where you can’t sleep, with police officers telling you that if you don’t talk, if you don’t tell the truth, threatening you, telling you that your life is going to be ruined,” he said.
“It’s an experience that can be deeply traumatic and is completely out of proportion.”
Amid a growing outcry, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez announced Wednesday that the model of stun grenade suspected of mutilating the teenager in Lens will no longer be used against high schoolers, in light, he said, of a “strong possibility” that such a weapon was involved in ripping off the pupil’s hand.
“We need to understand exactly what happened,” Nunez said.
Still, he has also defended police actions as proportionate in “almost all cases.” He says police have been obliged to intervene when protests led to rioting, vandalism and other violence, and have done so mindful that they’re largely dealing with children.
“You don’t handle a high schoolers’ movement in the same way as one by adults,” the minister said to broadcaster RTL.
In the case of the 14-year-old with a smashed jaw and teeth, the officer who fired his grenade launcher directly at him during a protest in Saint-Ouen l’Aumone, northwest of Paris, said during questioning in custody that he acted in “a fraction of a second” to protect a female colleague who’d exchanged blows with the boy, according to a statement from the prosecutor’s office leading the investigation.
It described the officer’s actions as disproportionate, resulting in a preliminary charge against him of violence by a public official causing mutilation or permanent disability. Suspended from duty and barred from carrying a gun, he is the first officer facing potential prosecution in 18 investigations opened so far into suspected police misconduct during the protests.
The boy, Eden, sent his mother a video from outside his school, showing police and some protesters, just moments before the officer shot him with the gas grenade, she said, speaking to The Associated Press and other media on condition that she not be identified to preserve the anonymity of her child.
But when she then called him, it was one of his classmates who answered, screaming that her son had been hit in the face and was on the ground, bleeding with his jaw and top teeth broken and bottom teeth “completely ripped out,” she said.
“It’s shameful, it’s appalling, it’s violent, it’s disgusting, it’s despicable — I could give you a whole list of words,” she said. “They are dealing with children. And children demanding what? Simply better conditions in which to study.”
In the crowds that demonstrated in Paris on Tuesday, marching boisterously from one city square to another, AP found three Paris-region teenagers who said they were arrested, handcuffed, searched, held in custody but then released with no criminal charges last week.
Samy and Warkya, both 17, said they were detained together with another friend. They believe that police picked on them because of their color. Warkya and the other friend are Black and Samy described himself as Arab. French officials have repeatedly denied that there is racism in the police ranks. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said in parliament this week that such accusations are “lies.”
Samy said the officers who stopped them said, “’You, you and you, you’re coming with us.’” There was no apparent motive, because “we weren’t wearing hoodies, we had nothing on us, our faces were visible,” he said.
“Here in France, they don’t listen to us. They would rather send in the police than listen to us and put measures in place to improve our daily lives,” he said.
Warkya said her first experience of police custody only reinforced her determination to protest but also taught her to run when officers appear.
“The police are more powerful than us,” she said. “There’s nothing we can do.”
