articles.title_orig: Comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and sea turtles prove nature loss can be reversed, scientists say
articles.title_zh: Comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and sea turtles prove nature loss can be reversed, scientists say
articles.content_orig:
A landmark report reveals that the world must change the way it produces food to avoid a biodiversity collapse
Conservation comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and green​ sea turtles prove that global nature loss can be reversed, ​scientists have said. ​But a report warns food production must be the next ​“positive tipping point​” if the world is to avert biodiversity collapse.
The World Wildlife Fund ( WWF ) analysed nearly 36,000 animal populations and more than 5,000 species, producing the largest ever database of vertebrate wildlife. Scientists found populations had declined by an average of 73% since 1970, showing that “nature continues to be degraded at an alarming scale”, with “no sign of losses slowing”.
Nature loss is no longer just an environmental challenge but a direct threat to the global economy, the report says, noting that about half of global GDP – roughly $58tn (£44tn) in 2023 – depends on nature and its ecosystem services. The authors write that species collapse now poses an “existential threat to economic stability, geopolitical security and human wellbeing”.
Animal populations were found to be falling most sharply in tropical, biodiversity-rich regions, while trends in northern temperate parts of the world appeared much gentler.
In Latin America and the Caribbean, land and freshwater wildlife populations fell by an average of 95% between 1970 and 2022, while the equivalent declines were 80% in Africa and 23% in Europe and Central Asia.
Freshwater wildlife suffered the sharpest losses across the world’s ecosystems, with monitored populations in rivers and lakes down by an average of 85%, compared with 69% for land species and 59% for marine species.
Tanya Steele, the chief executive of WWF UK, said: “Nature loss is not just a crisis for wildlife. It’s already sending us the bill through growing risks to our food security, water supplies, economy and resilience to climate shocks.
“We stand at a fork in the road: either we continue paying the rising price of nature loss, or we invest in nature’s recovery and a future where people and wildlife can thrive together.”
But despite the pattern of global biodiversity decline, wild tigers, green sea turtles and bluefin tuna are recovering, the report said, showing that “it is still possible to reverse the global loss of nature when action is taken”.
In 2010, about 3,200 wild tigers remained globally and the species was sliding toward extinction. After sustained and targeted conservation interventions, the population has grown to roughly 5,700, an increase of more than 70%.
Becci May, WWF UK’s tiger lead, said the remarkable comeback of wild tigers demonstrated the “science of hope” and proved that when climate and ecological action was taken, change was possible.
The report said Atlantic and Pacific bluefin tuna populations, which were collapsing after decades of overfishing, had now recovered to the point where neither was now considered threatened.
Last year, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle ever downlisted from endangered to “least concern” on the IUCN red list, reflecting 50 years of coordinated conservation work across about 80 countries.
Dr Mike Barrett, the chief scientific adviser for WWF UK and a co-author of the report, said: “These are examples that show that nature can recover even when pushed right to the brink, and they provide us with inspiration. It’s also very clear that conservation alone cannot tackle the scale of threats facing nature.”
He said nature would have no chance of recovery if “negative tipping points ” – self-reinforcing, irreversible ecological changes that accelerate climate crisis – were passed. “The systems which drive nature’s loss have to be transformed. And that’s energy, food and finance,” he said.
“Our report shows that we’ve already passed the tipping point in the energy sector with the take-up of renewable energy . That transition is now unstoppable. It’s not happening fast enough, but it is unstoppable.”
Humanity must likewise adapt the way it produces food, he said. “Agriculture is the single largest cause of habitat loss and degradation and therefore the loss of biodiversity. It’s also a major source of greenhouse gas emissions and so helps drive climate change, so you have that feedback.”
Dr Steve Smith, a research fellow from the University of Exeter and a co-author of the report, said: “The biggest prize for nature recovery would be a sustainable and healthy food system, but it’s currently the farthest away from positively tipping. For example, agricultural expansion drives almost 90% of deforestation worldwide.”
Positive tipping points are thresholds beyond which a sustainable technology or practice becomes increasingly cheap, widespread or politically popular, allowing progress to become self-propelling.

articles.title_orig: A hurricane could cripple US refining when the world can least afford it
articles.title_zh: A hurricane could cripple US refining when the world can least afford it
articles.content_orig:
The global energy system is already being pushed to the brink. A hurricane barreling down on America’s refining nerve center is the last thing that’s needed.
Isaias, the Atlantic season’s first hurricane , is arriving at a time when there is almost no margin for error.
US refineries, mostly located along the Gulf Coast, are running as hard as they can to offset war-driven outages overseas. Fuel inventories that act as shock absorbers have already been tapped. And America’s emergency oil stockpile is at the lowest level since 1982.
Hurricane Isaias “could be a gigantic event. It’s the worst time something like this could happen in 25 years,” said Robert Yawger, director of energy futures at Mizuho Securities.
The actual impact of Isaias will depend on the storm’s path and intensity.
Current forecasts call for the storm to hit east of New Orleans, a major refining hub, which should spare vital energy infrastructure from the storm’s worst.
Still, major oil producers including Shell, Chevron and BP have evacuated non-essential personnel from oil platforms in the Gulf and curtailed production .
As of midday Wednesday, about 512,000 barrels per day of Gulf of Mexico oil production had been shut in, according to the federal agency Marine Minerals Administration.
That amounts to about 25% of the region’s production. And about 16% of current natural gas production in the Gulf of Mexico has been sidelined.
The risk is that the storm’s damage could squeeze supply chains even more, further raising historically high prices.
The Iran war, combined with Ukrainian drone attacks in Russia and export restrictions in China, have catapulted diesel prices to all-time highs. Gasoline was more than $4.40 per gallon last week and has never been this expensive at this time of year.
About 2.7 million barrels per day, or 14%, of America’s refining capacity, lie within or near the projected of the path of the storm, according to Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates.
Lipow said he expects at least some refineries in the New Orleans/Baton Rouge and Mississippi/Alabama regions will have to slow down how much oil they turn into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
Tankers delivering oil to refineries and loading fuel out of refineries could get delayed as well. This would particularly impact Florida because the state relies on shipments of fuel from the Gulf Coast.
“There is no slack in the system to make up for lost refinery capacity. Lost production will have to come out of already low commercial inventories,” Lipow wrote in an email.
Those commercial inventories have been whittled away.
Gasoline stockpiles recently fell to their lowest seasonal record since 2012, according to federal data.
Distillate inventories, which include mostly diesel, are at their lowest level for early October since tracking started in the early 1980s.
Not only that, but the Strategic Petroleum Reserve has been aggressively drained to ease the energy shock. The SPR now holds about 283 million barrels of crude, the least since 1982 when the emergency reserve was being filled during the Reagan administration.
Refineries in the Middle East have been damaged by the Iran war, or have struggled to get shipments out to the rest of the world. Refineries in Russia have been destroyed or damaged by drone attacks. And China, seeking to avoid fuel shortages, has restricted its exports.
US refineries, operating at about 95% of their capacity, are one of the remaining key sources for the global fuel supply.
“It would be a disaster if US refining capacity has to come off the market. It would basically force a diesel export ban,” said Yawger, the Mizuho executive, who added that he is not in favor of restricting US diesel exports .
Much depends on the intensity of the storm, including the severity of flooding and wind damage. Isaias could peak as a Category 2 storm with 110 mph winds by early Friday, but is expected to weaken somewhat before landfall.
Even with a Category 1 hurricane, it can take a week to return refining operations to normal.

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests
articles.content_orig:
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage
Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally was rocked by repeated protests on Wednesday as the US president urged Texas voters to back embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted the US president during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena.
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage. “He’s going back home to mom,” the president said after the man was removed. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”
Supporters waving cowboy hats and chanting “USA” drowned out some of the protesters, while Trump told demonstrators to “get the hell out of here”. He mocked their appearance and claimed without evidence that “they’re paid by enemies of our nation”.
The president also used Wednesday’s rally to address recent comments in which he appeared to suggest that Iran could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego, earning widespread condemnation from Democrats.
In remarks that were again less than crystal clear, Trump said: “I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit – you want to see a horror show? You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles and you want to see some bad things happen.
“You want to see a country that would be in freefall. We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities, we protect our country, we’re not letting that happen. And they’d use it, too. They’d use it.”
Trump was making his third trip to Texas in less than a month as Republicans pour money into races they had expected to win comfortably in November’s midterm elections.
Paxton, whom Trump endorsed during the Republican primary after turning against the incumbent senator John Cornyn, was called on stage by the president and thanked him for his support.
“Mr President, I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas,” Paxton said. “We are going to win this race.”
Trump described Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America,” and said: “He was tough and he was with us all the way. He’s a fantastic man.”
The Republican campaign to maintain control of the Senate has become increasingly focused on Texas, where Democrat James Talarico has emerged as a serious threat. A New York Times/ Siena College poll released last weekend showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Texas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988.
Trump won the state by almost 14 percentage points in 2024, but his approval rating has fallen sharply. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday put his approval rating at 32%, while registered voters preferred Democrats to Republicans 44%-37%.
after newsletter promotion
Trump’s relationship with Paxton has sometimes appeared uneasy. Trump called Paxton “a pain in the ass sometimes” last week, but on Wednesday did not discuss a leaked recording of Paxton in which the Senate candidate reportedly complained about the war in Iran, rising fuel prices and the way his campaign was being run.
Instead he spent much of the rally attacking Talarico, whom he repeatedly referred to as “Tala-freako”. He claimed without evidence that Talarico is vegan and recently disappeared: “He’s sick because he’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”
Trump insisted: “The people of Texas are not going to let weak, gutless, self-hating, transgender-promoting freak shows destroy everything that we’ve built.”
The president’s political difficulties in Texas were underlined by the absence of Republican governor Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is himself facing a competitive re-election race against Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa.
Abbott was instead due to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on his decision not to appear with Trump.
Republicans have now devoted more than $300m to elections in Texas, according to the Associated Press, while Trump’s broader 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through several Republican-leaning states, including Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska.

articles.title_orig: Republican midterm triage puts bleak outlook into focus
articles.title_zh: Republican midterm triage puts bleak outlook into focus
articles.content_orig:
The biggest donors in the 2026 midterm election are breaking decisively toward Republican candidates and causes, a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records found.
Fourteen of the 20 largest donors and donor groups this election cycle have exclusively or nearly exclusively backed GOP candidates or aligned groups, according to a CNBC analysis of federal campaign-finance records. Together, the 20 account for $1.2 billion, or about an eighth of the roughly $9.8 billion raised this election cycle through Sept. 25 across the campaigns and super PACs CNBC examined.
CNBC analyzed FEC records for contributions reported during the 2026 election cycle, covering Jan. 1, 2025, through the latest filings available, combining spouses and closely affiliated donor entities where appropriate and removing duplicate or superseded transactions. The analysis of disclosed federal political committee contributions provides the most up-to-date snapshot of who is financing the 2026 midterms and shows a stark divide in where the biggest donors are putting their money.
Democratic megadonors, meanwhile, are increasingly bypassing the national party, though in some cases they're giving directly to candidates instead.
With less than four weeks until Election Day , some of the biggest six-figure checks that once routinely flowed to the Democratic National Committee haven't materialized. Fundraisers told CNBC the hesitation reflects lingering 2024 election "trauma" from Kamala Harris' defeat, fears of democratic socialism and disillusionment with the DNC's leadership in Washington.
"We don't have the kind of donors they've got," said Matt Bennett of the centrist Democratic think tank Third Way. "The advantages that the Republicans have are enormous, and no amount of donor enthusiasm on our side is going to close that gap."
The Republican Party is scrambling to defend its congressional majorities as more House and Senate races once considered safe for the GOP have become competitive. From Labor Day through Sept. 25, conservative super PACs have outspent their Democratic counterparts $310 million to $174 million, a magnitude approaching 2 to 1, according to CNBC's analysis of FEC records.
"No one ever agrees with anyone on 100% of the issues, but we are doing really well fundraising," said Republican fundraiser Eric Levine, founder and managing member of ERL Federal Consultants. "My understanding is that a lot of this money is going to candidates that may have a little trouble raising their own money. One name that comes to mind is [Ken] Paxton in Texas."
Less than six weeks before Election Day, the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter shifted 15 House races toward Democrats and said the GOP was on track to lose its House majority. The race for control of the Senate is closer but has also moved toward Democrats: Cook now rates control a " true Toss Up ," with Democrats needing four seats.
Democrats "are starting to see this real opportunity in a bunch of these races," said Caroline Welles , who leads The First Ask, a PAC supporting Democratic women, after working at the DNC from 2017 through 2022.
Republican money is coming from Wall Street financiers and industrial titans alongside a new wave of cryptocurrency , artificial intelligence and online gambling executives. The cash is flowing to candidates, super PACs and industry groups aiming to shape policy fights in Washington.
Nine of the 10 largest individual and family donors in CNBC’s overall top 20 groups are Republican-aligned, accounting for 86 cents of every dollar contributed by the top 10, according to CNBC's analysis of FEC records. The previously unreported finding is a sharp increase from a comparable point in the 2022 midterms, when Republican-aligned donors accounted for 67 cents of every dollar from the top 10.
"Populist sentiment against billionaires is at a fever pitch, but they have more money and more impact than ever before," said Saurav Ghosh , the Campaign Legal Center's director of federal campaign finance reform. "It's the result of unchecked free-for-all spending, and evidence has shown it can swing close races." The group is a nonpartisan nonprofit founded by a former Republican FEC chairman.
Seven of the 20 largest donors and donor groups in CNBC's analysis have major ties to the crypto, AI or online gambling industries. Together, they have contributed roughly $377.1 million this cycle, CNBC calculated — nearly a third of the money from the 20 largest donors and donor groups in CNBC's analysis.
Venture capitalists Marc Andreessen , Ben Horowitz and their firm Andreessen Horowitz have put roughly $91.3 million into politics this cycle. OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna , have given $50 million, while Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss have contributed roughly $55.1 million. Crypto.com operator Foris Dax Inc. has given $38.6 million. Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , whose businesses include xAI, is another top 20 donor.
Those four donor groups alone have contributed roughly $93 million to President Donald Trump's flagship super PAC, MAGA Inc. , which entered September with $415.8 million in cash after spending little of the $424.4 million it reported raising since Jan. 1, 2025. Two Trump-aligned groups launched in September, No Going Back PAC and Safety & Affordability PAC, have booked about $140 million in House and Senate ad buys and reservations, according to AdImpact.
Musk has contributed roughly $90.6 million during this cycle, including more than $50 million to his America PAC , according to CNBC's calculations based on FEC filings. His super PAC has since reported nearly $27 million in independent expenditures across House and Senate races in the 2026 general election, according to CNBC's analysis of FEC filings.
Companies are also directing millions into political groups focused on fights affecting their own industries.
Coinbase and Ripple have contributed roughly $33.2 million and $48 million, respectively, to crypto super PAC Fairshake , which supports candidates from both parties whom the industry considers allies. That's more than half of Coinbase's political spending and 96% of Ripple's this election. DraftKings has similarly directed about $34 million of its nearly $35 million spent this election to Win for America , the sports-betting industry's super PAC, according to FEC filings.
"Crypto wants to position itself as a political kingmaker — spending heavily and making sure lawmakers know it," said Dustin Duong , a researcher at Americans for Financial Reform who has analyzed crypto and AI political spending this election cycle. "But much of that money has gone to candidates already well-positioned to win."
In Congress, crypto companies are pushing for market-structure rules , AI firms are battling over how Washington will regulate their rapidly expanding industry, and sports-betting operators are confronting regulatory fights .
As Republican donors open their wallets, some of Democrats' biggest benefactors are missing from the DNC's donor rolls.
George Soros — the only Democratic-aligned donor among the 10 largest individual and family donor groups in CNBC's analysis— and his son Alex have given the DNC nothing this election cycle. It's a reversal from 2022, when the two contributed more than $1 million to the committee, according to FEC filings. The two gave $1.125 million combined to the DNC and its joint fundraising committee in 2022, a total that would have ranked first among DNC donors in CNBC's analysis.
Elsewhere, Dustin Moskovitz , the Facebook and Asana co-founder gave roughly $413,000 to the DNC during the 2024 cycle, alongside $50 million to Future Forward and $929,600 to the Harris Victory Fund . CNBC found no contribution from Moskovitz to the DNC this cycle.
"Donors, just like voters, want to feel energized and enthused, and they're getting that from the candidates this cycle rather than the major groups and the party apparatus," said The First Ask's Welle

articles.title_orig: Toss-ups, triage and targets: How to read the wide-open 2026 House map
articles.title_zh: Toss-ups, triage and targets: How to read the wide-open 2026 House map
articles.content_orig:
A general view of voting machines at the Franklin County Board of Elections on Oct. 6, 2026 in Columbus, Ohio. Jeff Dean/Getty Images hide caption
Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly .
With just under a month to go until Election Day, financial decisions made by both parties appear to suggest the question being asked is not if Democrats take control of the House, but how large the majority may be.
Currently, Republicans hold a narrow 218-214 seat advantage. In February 2025, the Cook Political Report's initial ratings for the midterms found a small slice of 39 races listed as competitive, with 18 classified as "toss-ups."
That topline number has shifted, with Cook currently listing 43 districts as competitive, including 22 toss-ups. But beyond that, under the hood, Democratic and Republican groups are marshalling hundreds of millions of dollars to influence an electoral landscape that is much larger.
An NPR analysis of both parties' campaign targets, future ad reservations and outside spending by Trump-aligned super PACs finds more than 90 districts where resources are being committed in the closing weeks of the midterms.
Here's a look at the types of races that will decide who controls the House in 2027.
If the political environment remained unchanged from the 2024 presidential election, a small group of House races would be competitive no matter what, like the 10 districts that voted for one party's presidential candidate and the other party's House nominee. (Not counting those changed by redistricting in the last 18 months, but more on that below.)
That includes the seats held by New York Republican Rep. Mike Lawler (NY-17), Pennsylvania Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-01) and Washington state Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (WA-03). Another group of seats had very close margins in 2024, like Democratic Rep. Adam Gray's victory by fewer than 200 votes in California's 13th Congressional District and a 799-vote victory for Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa's 1st Congressional District.
But this is not the same political environment as 2024. President Trump's unpopularity with voters has reached record highs, with the share of voters who strongly disapprove of his job performance sitting higher than any point in either term in office.
Voters are unhappy with the ongoing war in Iran, rising gas prices, tariffs and immigration enforcement, and a wave of anti-incumbent sentiment has driven a record number of congressional retirement announcements along with a number of sitting lawmakers losing their primary races this year.
Other races to watch: CO-08, NY-03, PA-08, PA-10
Further scrambling the map: a redistricting arms race that resulted in new district lines for an estimated 1 in 10 registered voters across several states.
Republican-led state legislatures, at Trump's urging and in some cases threats, tried to draw new House maps that would give them multiple additional seats in states like Texas and Florida, while Democrats countered in California.
But many of the new district lines were drawn with assumptions made about voters who backed President Trump in 2024 and what they would do in 2026, and in some cases, could backfire.
According to Strength in Numbers/Verasight polling data shared with NPR, Trump has lower-than-average job approval in communities that make up newly redrawn districts in South Florida and along the Texas-Mexico border, like TX-28 and FL-25.
In North Carolina's 1st Congressional District, Democrat Rep. Don Davis saw his district that Trump narrowly carried in 2024 become even more conservative. But the national environment — and a U.S. Senate race where polls show Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper leading — has made the contest more competitive. More than $20 million in ad reservations are scheduled between now and Election Day in the rural and coastal district, making it one of the most expensive House races in the country.
Other races to watch: AL-02, OH-09, FL-22, TX-35
Heading into the final electoral sprint, there are 60 districts that are listed as priorities of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the National Republican Congressional Committee along with Trump-aligned super PACs like No Going Back.
On average, those districts voted for Trump by an 8% margin in 2024, highlighting how deep into conservative areas competitive races have moved.
The DCCC has more than 90 districts on its battlefield map, including 46 targets to flip in its "Red To Blue" program, 26 "Frontline" incumbents in potentially tight races and another 19 it considers "Districts In Play."
The NRCC has 17 districts on its "Patriots" list of vulnerable incumbents to support and another 27 candidates in open races or challenging Democratic incumbents as part of the "MAGA Majority" program.
Not every race will ultimately end up close or see party control change hands. Many of the DCCC's "Districts In Play" gave Trump closer to 60% of the vote in 2024 and have seen little-to-no ad spend from either party.
Then, there are races like Kentucky's 6th Congressional District, where millions of dollars in spending has poured in from both parties — including from Trump-aligned super PACS — in a district Trump won by 15 points.
In Arkansas' 2nd Congressional District, which Trump also won by 15 points, six-figure outside spending targeting Democratic nominee Chris Jones and boosting incumbent Rep. French Hill contributed to the DCCC adding that race to its "Red To Blue" target.
According to Ballotpedia tracking, the target lists compiled by the DCCC and NRCC are usually broader in their scope and limited in their success. From 2012-2024, the Democrats won a total of 34% of its target districts and Republicans won 29%.
In some races and places, Republicans and Democrats are beginning to pull back ad reservations for the rest of the year, according to data from ad tracking firm AdImpact, though for different reasons. The most high profile example for Republicans is halting the flow of money in the North Carolina Senate race and redirecting funds to Kansas.
Some House races have seen similar cancellations, too, like the open race in Nebraska's 2nd District that is both a DCCC Red To Blue and NRCC MAGA Majority target.
Still, that data shows close to half a billion dollars in ad reservations have been placed between now and Election Day, showing that in this midterm election neither party is taking anything for granted.
Other races to watch: FL-13, NC-11, OH-10, OH-15

articles.title_orig: ‘Nature can recover’: Inside the race to rescue world’s crisis-hit wildlife
articles.title_zh: ‘Nature can recover’: Inside the race to rescue world’s crisis-hit wildlife
articles.content_orig:
Beneath the dense forest canopy of Uganda’s Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, a troop of gorillas is being quietly observed by a group of tourists who have each paid $800 for the privilege of the experience.
In villages around the park, a thriving economy has grown off the back of the gorillas’ presence here, from the sale of wood carvings to visitors and the provision of accommodation for up to 40,000 tourists a year.
In the national park, which sprawls along the edge of the Rift Valley and the border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), there are many local jobs for rangers and guides.
But deeper into the forest, more mountain gorillas live away from human contact, quietly enhancing the natural world around them through their daily routines of foraging, nest building and dispersing seeds.
And, crucially, by increasing their own populations.
In the 1980s, the mountain gorilla was on the fast track to extinction. Now, there are more than 1,100 living in thriving populations in Uganda, Rwanda and the DRC.
Theirs is a story of conservation success that spills beyond the species themselves, into the nature they live in, and the human communities they exist alongside.
“The mountain gorilla story shows us that conservation can work,” Tara Stoinski of the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund tells Al Jazeera. “It’s a really important example of the effort that’s needed to make that happen – decades of sustained conservation action that includes direct protection, science-informed management and meaningful community support and involvement.”
This is welcome news for a natural world beset by crisis.
According to this year’s Living Planet Report by the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), over the past 52 years, there has been a 73 percent decline in the average size of monitored wildlife populations. Across the world, habitats have been degraded and lost as overexploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive species take their toll.
But the report also highlights important recoveries in populations of green turtles, bluefin tuna, tigers and Southern African elephants. “For too long nature has been undervalued,” says Andrew Terry, chief conservation officer at the Zoological Society of London, who helped produce the report. “But these declines are not inevitable and change is possible. Nature can recover, and these stories are a powerful reminder of this.”
The WWF says these conservation successes demonstrate how international partnerships drive results. Intergovernmental commitments from tiger range countries, including India, Bhutan, Nepal, Laos and China, helped increase global wild tiger numbers by more than 70 percent between 2010 and 2025.
In 2025, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle ever to be downlisted from “endangered” to “least concern” on the International Union for the Conservation of Nature Red List. That reflected 50 years of species research, active protection of nesting females and eggs, measures to reduce fishing gear and sustained community engagement.
Professor Brendon Godley is a leading conservation scientist at the University of Exeter and the Sharjah Marine Research Centre in the United Arab Emirates and has spent much of his career dedicated to researching and protecting sea turtles. “Conservation success stories are hugely important because they demonstrate that declines are not inevitable,” he tells Al Jazeera.
“The recovery of species such as green turtles shows that when science, policy, enforcement and public support align, populations can rebound, sometimes remarkably so. However, they are not grounds for complacency.”
Indeed, these conservation triumphs are small battles won in an ongoing war against the degradation of nature. The WWF’s Living Planet Report highlights the three systems that are primarily driving the destruction of nature: the global food system, which is the leading cause of habitat loss as areas are cleared to grow crops; the energy system, which fuels climate change through burning fossil fuels; and the finance system, which bankrolls harmful activities, for example, large-scale infrastructure or mining projects.
Kirsten Schuijt, director general of WWF, says these industries and systems need to be transformed. “Progress is already under way,” she tells Al Jazeera. “Not everywhere, and not yet at the scale required, but enough to demonstrate that change is possible.”
The return of a species can have a powerful effect. In 2010, Atlantic bluefin tuna populations had declined by 80 percent and the species was listed as endangered. They had disappeared from much of their historical range, including UK waters. Yet today they are returning in numbers not witnessed in generations, perhaps ever.
“What makes this story particularly powerful is that the recovery is visible,” says Tom Horton, research fellow at the University of Exeter. “Coastal communities, fishers and sea-users who had never seen a bluefin tuna in British waters are now encountering them regularly. It transforms conservation from an abstract concept into something tangible.”
These successes serve as inspiration for other conservation projects in the fight against species decline, like that of the largest primate on Earth, the critically endangered Grauer’s Gorilla. Its home range lies within the vast remote forests of the DRC, living in a landscape beset by instability and habitat loss. Its numbers have dropped by an estimated 60 percent to just 6,800 today.
Urbain Ngobobo, country director for the Dian Fossey Fund in the DRC, explains that the challenge of restoring numbers there is significant but so is the opportunity.
“Every forest we help communities protect,” he says, “every gorilla we are able to monitor and every young Congolese person who develops the skills to become a conservation leader, represents progress.
“That is where hope comes from – not from assuming the future will be easy, but from knowing that our actions today can change what is possible tomorrow.”

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Federal Reserve Governor Chris Waller said in a speech Thursday that he expects the Fed will need to enact more interest rate hikes to bring down inflation faster if economic data comes in as he expects.
"If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2% goal," Waller said at the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye İstanbul Economic Forum. "But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
Waller noted a convergence of factors have gelled into persistent inflationary forces, including hopes for a quick ending to the Middle East conflict and warnings that low inventories and damaged infrastructure could keep oil prices high through 2027. He also pointed out that the artificial intelligence build-out has significantly driven up high-tech consumer prices , and projections of its size have ballooned. Additionally, he said, continuing trade conflicts threaten new tariffs that could put upward pressure on inflation yet again.
"When the first inflation reading for August came in hot just before the FOMC's September meeting, it was impossible to deny that inflation was still too high and not making sufficient progress toward our target," Waller said.

Waller sees economic activity strengthening in the second half of this year, and says he's "not greatly concerned" that higher interest rates threaten to markedly slow down the economy.
"But I am concerned that the recent acceleration in inflation — after what soon will be five and a half years of it above the FOMC's target — will lead consumers, investors, and price-setting businesses to revise up their expectations for future inflation."
He noted that he sees the economy in roughly the same place as it was at the time of the Fed's policy meeting in mid-September.
"Overall, the new data reinforce my view that the labor market is stable and inflation is too high," he said. "For at least the near term, policy will be focused on the inflation side of our mandate."
Waller also made a point of sharing how he believes the Fed should communicate its interest rate expectations . He doesn't think choosing to say nothing or offering a strong indication of what the Fed will do is how the central bank should communicate. Rather, he believes an in-between approach of signaling the amount of rate hikes over some time interval, while not saying what the pace of hikes will be or how large they will be, would offer flexibility, while keeping the public informed.
"We could emphasize that the course of monetary policy is not predetermined and will depend on incoming data," he said.
"Policymakers could signal where they are likely headed while acknowledging that there is no fixed final destination — except for the achievement of price stability and maximum employment."

articles.title_orig: Kiplimo and Feysa return to defend Chicago titles
articles.title_zh: Kiplimo and Feysa return to defend Chicago titles
articles.content_orig:
Jacob Kiplimo and Hawi Feysa in Chicago ( © Bank of America Chicago Marathon Kevin Morris )
Jacob Kiplimo and Hawi Feysa will return to the Bank of America Chicago Marathon to defend their titles against deep international fields at the World Athletics Platinum Label road race on Sunday (11).
Kiplimo heads back to Chicago having significantly improved his marathon credentials since winning there 12 months ago, while Feysa faces a women’s field that includes former world record-holder Brigid Kosgei and two-time Boston champion Sharon Lokedi.
Kiplimo won in Chicago last year in 2:02:23, finishing more than a minute ahead of Kenya’s Amos Kipruto in what was just the Ugandan’s second race over the distance.
He has since enjoyed a remarkable 2026. After claiming his third consecutive title at the World Cross Country Championships, he broke the world half marathon record with 57:20 in Lisbon – a mark that has since been improved – and then produced another breakthrough over 26.2 miles.
At April’s London Marathon, Kiplimo finished third in 2:00:28 as Sabastian Sawe and Yomif Kejelcha became the first two men to officially break two hours for the distance. Kiplimo’s time put him third on the world all-time list and improved his own Ugandan record by almost two minutes.
It is also seven seconds faster than the Chicago course record of 2:00:35 set by the late Kelvin Kiptum in 2023.
“My preparation has given me a lot of confidence, and having raced this course before is a real advantage,” said Kiplimo.
He will renew his rivalry with Kipruto, who followed him home in Chicago last year and then finished one place behind him in London in April. The 2022 London champion clocked a PB of 2:01:39 on that occasion, making him the second-fastest man in a field that includes six sub-2:04 performers.
Milkesa Mengesha, the 2024 Berlin Marathon champion, returns to the USA after finishing 10th in Boston in April. The Ethiopian has a best of 2:03:17. His compatriot Tadese Takele retained his Tokyo Marathon title in March in 2:03:37. Kenya’s Daniel Mateiko was fourth in that race in a PB of 2:03:44 and will also line up in Chicago.
Another Ethiopian, Asrar Hiyrden, completes the group of sub-2:04 entrants. He ran 2:03:59 in Seville in February.
Several athletes just outside that group will be looking to make another step forward. USA’s Charles Hicks ran 2:04:35 to finish seventh at the Boston Marathon in April, while Suguru Osako holds the Japanese record of 2:04:55.
Hicks is part of a strong US contingent that also includes Clayton Young, who ran 2:05:41 in Boston, 2017 Chicago champion Galen Rupp and Vincent Mauri, whose 2:05:54 victory in Toledo earlier this year marked a major breakthrough.
South Africa’s Adriaan Wildschutt, Japan’s Tomoki Ota and Thailand’s Kieran Tuntivate – all of whom hold national records at other distances – are among the athletes making their marathon debuts.
While Feysa is the defending women’s champion, Kosgei has perhaps the strongest historical connection with the Chicago course.
The Kenyan won there in 2018 before returning the following year to clock 2:14:04, taking 81 seconds off Paula Radcliffe’s long-standing world record. She has not raced in Chicago since that performance.
Now 32, Kosgei has returned to some of her best form this year. She won the Tokyo Marathon in March in 2:14:29 – the second-fastest time of her career and an Asian all-comers’ record.
Feysa was third in that race in 2:17:39, having enjoyed the biggest victory of her career in Chicago five months earlier. The Ethiopian pulled away from the field to win the 2025 race in 2:14:57, more than two minutes ahead of compatriot Megertu Alemu.
Alemu returns this year, as does Sutume Kebede, whose 2:15:55 PB makes her the third-fastest woman in the field. Both raced in Tokyo earlier this year, where Kebede and Alemu finished fourth and fifth respectively.
Lokedi, meanwhile, will race in Chicago for the first time. The Kenyan has established herself as one of the world’s leading championship-style marathon racers, having won the New York Marathon in 2022 before taking back-to-back Boston titles in 2025 and 2026.
She retained her Boston crown in April in 2:18:51, with two more Chicago entrants – Loice Chemnung and Mary Ngugi-Cooper – completing the podium. Chicago will provide Lokedi with her first opportunity to race one of the flatter, faster courses on the major marathon circuit.
Brillian Kipkoech is another Kenyan arriving on the back of a victory. She improved her PB to 2:17:05 to win in Hamburg in April and is one of seven women in the field with a best inside 2:18. Degitu Azimeraw, the 2021 London runner-up, is another member of that group. Chemnung, Joan Kilimo, Magdalyne Masai, Fantu Worku and Ngugi-Cooper have all broken 2:20.
Kilimo, just 22, achieved her 2:18:40 best when finishing runner-up in Barcelona in March, while Worku ran 2:19:08 for third in Dubai at the start of February.
The home challenge includes Susanna Sullivan, Natosha Rogers, Sara Hall and Dakotah Popehn. Emma Grace Hurley, meanwhile, is among the intriguing debutantes. She returns to Chicago having set a US 8km record at the Shamrock Shuffle earlier this year, while Mexico’s Laura Galvan and Great Britain’s Amy-Eloise Neale will also contest their first marathons.

articles.title_orig: Russia dismisses reports of second plague case as ‘false information’
articles.title_zh: Russia dismisses reports of second plague case as ‘false information’
articles.content_orig:
What we know about Russia’s suspected plague case
Russia has dismissed media reports of a second suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia, as the World Health Organization (WHO) urged Moscow to formally respond to its inquiry regarding the reports.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday that “the vast majority of what the media is reporting regarding this situation is false information”, in response to a question about reports of a second case.
Peskov said that information on the suspected cases should be derived from official statements by Russia’s health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor.
Russia’s health regulator said there were no infections detected among staff after a plague institute worker died from pneumonia. The origin of the illness remains unknown, prompting international concern that the case could involve the plague.
Russia acknowledged on Sunday that a 28-year-old woman employed at a plague research institute in Siberia’s Irkutsk died after she was diagnosed with a “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, prompting global concern over a suspected plague case.
The United States, the European Union and the WHO have all called on Russia to be transparent about the situation.
US President Donald Trump told reporters on Wednesday when asked whether it’s possible the infection was from a bioweapon, “We do not think so.”
“They are saying it is very much under control,” he said, adding “Russia is not saying much either.”
Trump confirmed he has spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and when asked about what US intelligence agencies are reporting, Trump said the two sides are “in very deep discussions” and that they would likely be able to provide an update “probably tomorrow.”
WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged Russia to clarify “media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause” at the Irkutsk institute.
“We have received information from two media outlets, one of them is Russian,” Tedros said in a briefing on Wednesday, adding, “We asked Russia to respond to that.”
“We cannot ignore any reporting that comes,” the WHO chief said.
WHO Director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management Maria Van Kerkhove said the UN agency does not know the “causative agent” behind the death in the first suspected case.
In a briefing, Van Kerkhove said, “We don’t understand how she was infected.”
“We need information in a timely way. We need regular information. We need answers to the follow-up of the questions that we have asked,” she added.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) described the risk to the United States from the suspected pneumonic plague case as “extremely low”.
CDC Director Erica Schwartz said on Wednesday that the US agency is working with the departments of Homeland Security, State, Defense and other agencies to monitor people travelling from the area.
The CDC has a health station at New York City’s John F Kennedy International Airport that can screen travellers coming from the Siberian region, she added.
About 200 people per year travel from the Siberian region to the United States, a Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson told the Reuters news agency.
Direct flights between Russia and the US have been suspended since the start of the Ukraine war in 2022.
“What we’re doing from a whole of government standpoint is we’re making sure that we understand exactly what that threat is,” Schwartz said at the Wall Street Journal’s The Future of Health event in Washington, DC.
“At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” the CDC said in a separate statement.

articles.title_orig: Ten years later, Penn’s Perry World House continues to shape global policy
articles.title_zh: Ten years later, Penn’s Perry World House continues to shape global policy
articles.content_orig:
Ten years after Perry World House opened its doors at Penn, the center has adapted to a changing world while retaining its founding mission.
PWH opened in September 2016 following a $10 million gift three years earlier from 1977 Wharton graduate and then-Trustee Richard Perry and his wife, Lisa. Since then, the center has expanded its reach across campus while engaging students, scholars, and policymakers.
In an interview, Political Science professor and PWH Faculty Director Michael Horowitz — who has long been affiliated with the center — said that former Penn President Amy Gutmann envisioned PWH as a way to bring together expertise on global policy issues across Penn’s 12 schools.
The goal, he said, was to “make the whole bigger than the sum of the parts in a way that could create transformational experiences” for the Penn community. In preparation for that role, PWH began its programming even before its physical space opened.
The building replaced the Kappa Alpha Society’s old house on Locust Walk. Most of the old building was torn down, leaving “a huge hole in the ground” during construction , Horowitz explained.

“While all of that construction was going on from 2014 to 2016, World House was starting to ramp up programming across the University,” he added.
Just a year after its opening, the center received nearly $500,000 from the Carnegie Corporation of New York — now known as the Andrew Carnegie Foundation — to assist its Global Innovation Program. The grant-funded workshops and initiatives focused on interdisciplinary conversation and international policy issues.
Over the following years, the center broadened both its programming and its network.
Perry World House panel celebrates Benjamin Franklin’s role at Constitutional Convention
Perry World House announces inaugural cohort of faculty research fellows
“The mission of World House has always been the same,” Horowitz said, describing its focus as “bridging the gap between academia and the policy world.”
One example is its Distinguished Visiting Fellows Program, a key avenue for connecting Penn students and faculty with policymakers, government officials, and scholars from around the world. The program, which has existed since PWH’s inception, has a cohort of 14 global leaders this academic year.
While its institutional values have remained steady, other aspects of PWH have changed over time.
When it first opened, the center’s work focused on two broad themes: global order and global shifts. In summer 2024, the center reorganized its work around security, climate change, global justice and human rights, and democracy.
“World House is an institution that is supposed to reflect a changing world, and so what we do reflects that as well,” Horowitz said.
Political Science professor Beth Simmons, a member of PWH’s faculty council, said the change was intended to give the center “a little more precision” in what it focused on. She explained that the revised structure better matched the faculty, visiting fellows, and other resources the center has built over time.
“When it was first established, it had no built-in networks or anything like that — those had to be developed over time,” Simmons said. “It took true dedication by the staff, by the University to fund the efforts, by the faculty, by various people who have come in contact with the Perry World House.”
Faculty involvement has expanded alongside the center’s growth. According to Horowitz, PWH engaged more than 200 faculty members from all 12 of Penn’s schools during the last academic year.
The center also recently launched a Faculty Fellows program built around its four research areas.
“These faculty fellow projects are a way for World House to not just build broad relationships with lots of faculty, but deep relationships with faculty who are already doing transformational research,” Horowitz said. “What World House can help them do is connect with the global policy world to have impact.”
Student engagement is also a central part of PWH’s work, with three distinct programs offered. One of them, the World House Student Fellows program, includes 31 students from all four of Penn’s undergraduate schools this year.
Students participate in weekly seminars, work on yearlong policy projects, and travel to meet policymakers and other global affairs professionals.
College senior Ashti Tiwari, a World House Student Fellow and former staffer for The Daily Pennsylvanian, said that the program has shaped much of her experience at Penn.
“Places like Perry World House help you make sense of the world and the global issues of the world,” she said.
She also pointed to the interdisciplinary nature of the center.
“They really do try to bring people together from all parts of campus,” Tiwari said.
Evan Stubbs, a College senior who was previously a World House Student Fellow and a DP staffer, said the program gave him opportunities to engage directly with international policy organizations.
“I don’t know if those opportunities would really exist without Perry World House facilitating the connections and guiding people’s interests,” Stubbs said.
Through PWH, he had the opportunity to travel to Washington, New York, and Geneva. He also worked on a policy project with the United Nations Institute for Disarmament Research.
Stubbs also said that the program serves a “dual purpose” by helping students pursue policy opportunities they are passionate about while also giving organizations a way to recruit Penn students.
As PWH enters its second decade, Horowitz said that further increasing student involvement will be a priority.
“Our task over the next decade is to continue to integrate Penn students even more into our thinking and programming and activities in a way that helps create transformational opportunities to help shape not just people’s careers, but how they think,” he said.

articles.title_orig: World Health Organization says Russian lab worker’s death has not been clearly linked to plague
articles.title_zh: World Health Organization says Russian lab worker’s death has not been clearly linked to plague
articles.content_orig:
Frank McGeorge, MD , Local 4's Medical Expert
The World Health Organization says Russian authorities have reported no plague cases in the Irkutsk region.
The worker’s cause of death remains unclear.
A worker at a Siberian research institute that studies plague died after developing pneumonia, prompting officials to monitor and quarantine people who had contact with her and renewing questions about a disease many associate with the Middle Ages.
But Russian authorities have reported no plague cases in the region.
The World Health Organization said Russian officials described the worker’s illness as initially resembling a typical acute respiratory viral infection.
Officials have not publicly established the cause of death.
The worker died Oct. 2 at a hospital near Irkutsk, according to Reuters.
About 200 people who had contact with her were quarantined, and a local official said 60% had since been released.
Russian officials said no plague was found among the contacts who had been tested.
The WHO said it has been in contact with Russian authorities. Reports of the death have fueled speculation online, but Reuters reported there is no public evidence supporting the theories circulating on social media.
The incident has also revived memories of COVID-19.
But plague is not a new or unidentified disease. COVID-19 was caused by a newly identified virus; plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, a well-studied bacterium that persists in animal populations in parts of Africa, Asia and the Americas.
Dr. Leonard Johnson said plague persists in animal populations and continues to cause sporadic human cases around the world, including in the United States.
The CDC has said there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States from the Russian case.
There are three main forms of plague.
Bubonic plague, the most common, typically follows the bite of an infected flea and causes swollen lymph nodes.
Septicemic plague affects the blood; both it and bubonic plague are generally acquired through infected fleas.
Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and can spread through respiratory droplets from an infected person or animal, usually with close contact.
Pneumonic plague can be highly fatal if untreated, said Dr. Leonard Johnson, chief of infectious diseases at Henry Ford St. John Hospital.
But modern antibiotics can treat plague when given promptly. Johnson said people identified as close contacts of a confirmed case could be given preventive antibiotics, including doxycycline or ciprofloxacin, to reduce the chance of secondary infections.
He said the risk of wider spread remains low, particularly in the United States. That is a sharp contrast with the medieval epidemics that killed millions.
Experts remain cautious because they do not have direct access to the underlying information, and public statements by Russian authorities have not clearly established the cause of death.
So far, however, reports do not confirm plague or indicate a wider outbreak.

articles.title_zh: Microsoft Launches $2,599 Surface Laptop Ultra to Take on MacBook Pro
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft today announced launch timing and pricing for the Surface Laptop Ultra that it unveiled earlier this year.
The 15-inch Surface Laptop Ultra is priced starting at $2,599, undercutting Apple's $2,999 16-inch MacBook Pro , and it targets the same creator and developer market. Microsoft says it is built for "demanding creative, software development, AI, engineering, and 3D workloads."
Microsoft's new laptop uses an Nvidia RTX Spark chip, which includes an Nvidia Blackwell RTX GPU with up to 6,144 cores and an Nvidia Grace CPU with up to 20 cores. It supports up to 128GB of unified memory and has a new thermal architecture to support the hardware. The RTX Spark is an Arm-based chip, so the laptop runs Windows on Arm with x86 apps using Microsoft's Prism emulation.
According to Microsoft, the Surface Laptop Ultra is its most powerful notebook to date. It has the "brightest, sharpest, and most vivid display" Microsoft has used in a Surface device, with peak HDR brightness that's 25% higher than the M5 ‌MacBook Pro‌'s. The mini-LED display is a touchscreen, and it supports gestures and navigation, but not pen input.
The laptop is lighter than the 16-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌, with a large haptic trackpad and upgradeable storage. Microsoft even adopted a MagSafe equivalent, adding support for Magnetic Connect. Microsoft says Magnetic Connect is the "world's first built-in magnetic USB-C charging on a laptop." The device has three USB-C ports, a USB-A port, an HDMI port, an SD card reader, and a 3.5mm headphone jack.
Along with the Surface Laptop Ultra, Microsoft announced the $5,999 Surface RTX Spark Dev Box to compete with devices like the Mac Studio and Mac mini . It is equipped with an Nvidia RTX Spark chip and offers up to 1 petaflop of AI performance with support for AI models up to 120B parameters.
Microsoft is offering a bonus to customers who "break up" with their MacBooks. MacBook owners can get up to $1,000 cash back when purchasing a Surface Laptop Ultra by trading in an eligible MacBook. The Surface Laptop Ultra launches on October 16.
"We're confident that once today's creators and developers experience everything Surface Laptop Ultra has to offer, they won't look back," reads Microsoft's website.
The Surface Laptop Ultra will directly compete with Apple's rumored OLED MacBook, which could also have an Ultra name. The MacBook Ultra is expected to feature a touchscreen, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, and a thinner and lighter design.

articles.title_orig: World of Warcraft: Forever- The Future of Skyborne Visual Updates
articles.title_zh: World of Warcraft: Forever- The Future of Skyborne Visual Updates
articles.content_orig:
The World of Warcraft development team began our journey into World of Warcraft: Forever with ambitions that grew and evolved over time. Our aim has always been to uphold the original WoW era aesthetic, while giving players more choice in how they experience Azeroth.
Over the course of development, we have been aligning on the right range of fidelity and what feels like it belongs in the WoW: Forever world and what does not. The team has learned much in the process, and that will continue to strengthen more with future content.
Along the way, there were some ideas the team wanted to explore that ultimately didn’t quite meet the consistency and cohesion we are aiming for. To align with our goals better, we are taking aim at updating some of those visuals for the future. Here is one example of how we are revisiting the High Definition (HD) Skyborne Druid forms.
We removed a bit of the softness, added more detailed fur textures, and adjusted the color saturation. The Skyborne are from an exotic environment, and their Druid forms reflect that, but we don't want that to be dissonant with the visual language of other creatures in the world.
In choosing to offer an SD or HD toggle for player characters, we focused on the pre-existing races from original World of Warcraft since many people have an attachment to those models. However, we have heard feedback that the HD Skyborne can be jarring by contrast when placed in the same world as the SD models and world, and we agree.
So, for those of us that prefer the look of SD models and want more choice, Skyborne player characters (and yes SD Druid forms) are in development and arriving early 2027. We look forward to sharing more information closer to that date. For now, here is an early work in progress image.
This is just the start of our journey, and the whole team is thrilled with the reception for World of Warcraft: Forever . As we continue refining this vision together, we look forward to what lies ahead—for the Horde! For the Alliance! Forever!

A 1,000-mile-long (1,600 kilometers) Martian cloud that emerges and then quickly disappears from the Red Planet's sky nearly every day is even weirder than scientists realized. New simulations suggest that the eerie apparition can only be explained using "exotic physics" that have been theorized but never seen on Earth or anywhere else in the solar system .
The mysterious floating mass, dubbed the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC), frequently emerges above Arsia Mons , a 12-mile-tall (20 km) extinct volcano located in the Tharsis region , just south of the Red Planet's equator. The water vapor cloud was first spotted in 2018 by the European Space Agency's Mars Express orbiter and has since appeared nearly every morning throughout Mars' spring and summer, when increased solar radiation triggers strong surface winds. But it lasts only a few hours each day, before fully evaporating.
The AMEC can stretch up to 1,100 miles (1,800 km) long, around one-twelfth of Mars' circumference. For context, that is roughly twice the length of the U.K. or the distance between New York City and Miami.
Although the Red Planet is no stranger to giant dust clouds and occasional "iridescent streaks" of carbon dioxide , it is almost completely devoid of atmospheric water vapor. That makes it extremely rare for puffy, Earth-like clouds to form there, let alone ones so vast. As a result, scientists have struggled to explain this whacky weather.
But in a new study published Wednesday (Oct. 7) in the journal Nature Geoscience , researchers used Mars Express data to create new simulations in an effort to finally explain the AMEC. Initially, the team struggled to recreate the puzzling phenomenon. But when they abandoned traditional meteorological principles in favor of a more out-of-the-box explanation, they were eventually successful.
The AMEC forms when summer winds push water vapor up and over the 12-mile-high slopes of Arsia Mons. But it only lasts for a couple of hours at a time.
"To create the AMEC in our modelling, we found that we needed to include some exotic physics … physics that, while included in textbooks, is treated as theoretical and usually thought not to happen in nature," study first author Jorge Hernández-Bernal , a planetary scientist at the University of the Basque Country in Spain who was affiliated with Sorbonne University in Paris at the time of the study, said in a statement . "Once we included this physics in our simulations, the AMEC emerged just as we hoped."
The AMEC is an orographic cloud , meaning it forms as strong winds push water vapor up and over a raised structure, such as a mountain. Similar clouds also exist on Earth, including the "Levanter" cloud, which occasionally forms above the Rock of Gibraltar in southern Europe. However, the Martian equivalent cannot be explained by the same processes that occur on our planet.

On Earth, clouds form via a process called heterogeneous nucleation, in which moist air cools and condenses into ice crystals that form around tiny atmospheric particles, such as dust, salt, pollen or soot. But while Mars has plenty of atmospheric dust, that's not what's happening there.
"For the AMEC, it seems that cloud formation takes place without needing any of this 'stuff' [in the air]," said Hernández-Bernal, who has been studying the AMEC for the past six years. "Water vapour turns directly into icy cloud particles without any middle step. It's akin to droplets of condensation appearing in the middle of a room, rather than on a window."
The researchers call this "homogeneous nucleation" and say it has never been seen before in a planetary atmosphere. "It's wholly unexpected," Hernández-Bernal added.
Arsia Mons is the second-tallest volcano on Mars behind Olympus Mons, but is twice as tall as Mount Everest. This image, captured by NASA's Odyssey orbiter, helps give a scale of how huge the Martian mountain really is.
Other scientists previously predicted that homogeneous nucleation could occur in Earth's upper atmosphere or in the skies above Venus . However, this has been deemed highly unlikely because it requires humidity levels roughly 100,000 times greater than those on our planet's surface.
Given that modern-day Mars is almost completely devoid of water, it may seem unlikely that its humidity levels could reach such lofty heights. However, the Mars Express data tells a different story.
As wind rises up the slopes of Arsia Mons, which is more than twice as tall as Mount Everest , it creates a powerful wave that shoots air into the upper atmosphere at tremendous speed. The researchers calculated that the temperature of this air can drop by up to 54 degrees Fahrenheit (30 degrees Celsius) in just 10 minutes. This not only makes it easy to freeze but also greatly increases the humidity within the wave, allowing homogeneous nucleation to take place, the simulations show.
So where does all this water come from? Some of it is already in the atmosphere, but some likely originates at the summit of Arsia Mons, which is covered with a thick layer of frost , the researchers suggested.
The new simulations mark a big step forward in our understanding of the AMEC and wider Martian meteorology.
"We don't have nearly as much information about Mars' atmosphere as we do about Earth's, so reproducing the AMEC to this degree is a big success for the model," Hernández-Bernal said.
Mars Express has been closely monitoring the AMEC since 2018. These photos show the cloud appearing over consecutive days in July 2020.
The findings would not have been possible without the Mars Express orbiter, which used three instruments — the Visual Monitoring Camera, the High Resolution Stereo Camera and the OMEGA instrument — to map out how the AMEC takes shape and evolves every day. It is also one of the only Mars spacecraft that can see Arsia Mons in daylight.
"Mars Express discovered the AMEC, has followed up and monitored it for years, and is now helping reveal the secrets of its formation," Colin Wilson , the project scientist for Mars Express, who was not involved in the new study, said in the statement.
The discovery is also a reminder that, despite sharing the same basic principles, weather systems do not behave the same on other worlds as they do on Earth, which could have big implications for solar system exploration and the hunt for extraterrestrial life on distant exoplanets .

articles.title_orig: How PvP Progression in World of Warcraft: Forever Works
articles.title_zh: How PvP Progression in World of Warcraft: Forever Works
articles.content_orig:
Whether you’re charging into battlegrounds with your faction or setting your sights on long-term PvP (Player vs. Player) goals, World of Warcraft: Forever brings a refreshed sense of purpose to every match-up. This approach gives players more reasons to take part throughout the season while preserving the spirit of competition that defined PvP in the original World of Warcraft .
When reimagining the PvP system, we wanted to keep the design pillar of “Approachable and Familiar” firmly in view: simplifying the original Honor System while staying true to its roots.
In World of Warcraft: Forever, PvP progression has two parts: Honor and Rank Points.
Honor is a currency players earn through taking part in PvP content. This includes defeating other players, completing battlegrounds, and finishing relevant PvP quests. Players also earn increased Honor in highlighted battlegrounds during their holiday weeks.
As part of these updates, we reviewed Honor gains across battlegrounds so acquisition rates are more consistent across the board. We want players to enjoy the full range of battleground maps without feeling compelled to choose Alterac Valley solely for Honor efficiency.
Rank Points come from PvP activities such as battlegrounds and relevant PvP quests, with holiday-week battlegrounds offering an additional boost. As players earn Rank Points, they advance through familiar PvP ranks from original World of Warcraft, working toward the ultimate titles of High Warlord for the Horde or Grand Marshal for the Alliance. Ranks have a weekly cap, retaining the foundation of the original system while making the journey more accessible.
Honor can be used to purchase two sets of PvP gear: one blue-quality set and one epic-quality set. The epic set requires the blue piece plus an Emboldened Seal to upgrade it, and Emboldened Seals have rank requirements players must reach before purchasing. There are also new and reworked items to fill gaps for specializations that were previously missing options. For example, Shaman now have healer, melee, and caster PvP gear sets they can acquire.
Below are the rank requirements for PvP item rewards:
Rank 1 - Tabard Rank 2 - PvP Trinket Rank 3 - Cloaks Rank 4 - Necklace Rank 5 - Combat Potions Rank 6 - Tabard Rank 7 - Battle Standard Rank 8 - Epic Bracers/Epic Belt Upgrade Token Rank 9 - Epic Boots Upgrade Token Rank 10 - Epic Gloves Upgrade Token Rank 11 - Mounts Rank 12 - Epic Legs/Epic Shoulders Upgrade Token Rank 13 - Epic Chest/Epic Helm Upgrade Token Rank 14 - Epic Weapons
To view your progress, you can open your Character Pane (Hotkey-C) then select the Player vs. Player tab on the right side of the interface. It will show you your rank, your current Rank Points, and what rewards are available for purchase based on your rank.
During a PvP season, players can progress through the ranks and earn Honor. Each season also includes a journey with weekly tasks to complete. Successfully completing those tasks grants Honor and Rank Points, and three tasks each season also grant a Legacy Point. Completing these tasks is part of the seasonal journey, and because they are tied to the Legacy System, they remain available to complete in future seasons.
With more ways to make progress each week and meaningful goals to pursue throughout the season, PvP in World of Warcraft: Forever gives players a clear path to jump in, compete, and keep building toward what comes next.

articles.title_orig: Space station crew heads home as replacements settle in for 6-month tour of duty
articles.title_zh: Space station crew heads home as replacements settle in for 6-month tour of duty
articles.content_orig:
The four people departing the International Space Station strapped into their Crew Dragon capsule and undocked early Wednesday, setting up re-entry and splashdown Thursday off the coast of Southern California to close out a 237-day stay in orbit.
With Crew 12 commander Jessica Meir and pilot Jack Hathaway at the controls, flanked on their left by European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and on the right by cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev, the Crew Dragon "Freedom" backed away from the space-facing port on the forward Harmony module at 8:05 a.m. Eastern Time.
Sailing 260 miles above Cuba and the Bahamas, the capsule executed an automated loop over the top of the lab complex and slowly dropped away behind, exiting the safety zones around the station.
"We just wanted to give an enormous thank you to all of the team, our friends and colleagues on board the International Space Station, everybody in Houston, everybody at SpaceX, all around the world, with all of our international partners," Meir radioed as the Crew Dragon departed. "We have had the most incredible of expeditions ... and we will never forget it, and never forget all of your hard work."
After enjoying a final day in weightlessness, Meir and Hathaway will monitor a nine-minute and 20-second firing of the Crew Dragon's forward Draco thrusters starting at 10:46 a.m. ET on Thursday, setting up a fiery plunge back to Earth and splashdown off the coast of California at 11:34 a.m. ET.
Left behind aboard the space station were the Crew 13 fliers that replaced them — commander Jessica Watkins, pilot Luke Delaney, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk and cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov — who were launched to the station on Oct. 1.
Also on board are Soyuz MS-29 commander Pyotr Dubrov, cosmonaut Anna Kikina and NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan on July 14. They plan to remain aboard the station for eight months while Crew 13 is planning a six-month tour of duty.
In a brief ceremony Sunday, Meir turned command of the station over to Dubrov, saying Crew 12's departure would mark a "bittersweet" moment.
"We will be leaving our friends," she said. "But we know that we are going home to our friends, to our families, to all of our team members on the ground. So it's a lot of mixed, swirling emotions for all of us when one leaves a home like this up on the space station."
She presented a symbolic "key to the space station" to Dubrov, who said "it's a great honor and a great responsibility to be the commander of such a magnificent place like International Space Station."
"It has a special meaning for me today, because 69 years ago on this day (Oct. 4) the first Sputnik was launched. Today is the dawn of the space era for humanity, and International Space Station is the greatest symbol of what we can do if we work together."
The combined crews then gathered in a group hug, or "huggle," as Meir described it, forming a circle with arms around each other's shoulders.
With splashdown Thursday, Meir, Hathaway, Adenot and Fedyaev will wrap up a 237-day and five-hour mission, flying around the planet 3,792 times and logging nearly 101 million miles from start to finish.
Meir, wrapping up her second flight to the space station, will have logged a total of 442 days in space, completing four spacewalks during the Crew 12 mission and three during an earlier stay. Adenot carried out three back-to-back spacewalks of her own, including one with Meir and two with Menon.
